anchor_text: As procurator to your excellence
summary: A 'procurator' is a legal agent authorized to act in another's name — here, to marry on the king's behalf. Suffolk stood in for Henry VI at the wedding ceremony in Tours, a standard arrangement when a king could not travel to his bride's country. The real marriage took place once Margaret arrived in England.
detail: Proxy marriage (marriage by procurator) was a recognized legal institution in European courts. The proxy stood at the altar, said the vows, and sometimes even completed a formal 'bedding' ceremony fully clothed. Holinshed records that Suffolk, then Marquess of Suffolk, married Margaret in Henry VI's name at Tours in May 1444. Suffolk's kneeling delivery of Margaret to the king in the opening lines re-enacts the formal transfer of the bride from agent to principal.

anchor_text: Deliver up my title in the queen
summary: Suffolk's 'title in the queen' means his legal claim or right over her as her proxy husband. By kneeling and transferring her to Henry, he formally relinquishes that proxy authority. The phrase 'substance / Of that great shadow I did represent' elaborates the metaphor: Suffolk was only a stand-in ('shadow'), and Henry the real king ('substance') he represented.

anchor_text: mine alder-liefest sovereign
summary: 'Alder-liefest' is an intensified superlative meaning 'most beloved of all' — 'alder' here derives from the Old English genitive plural 'ealra' (of all). Margaret is addressing Henry as the sovereign she loves above all others. The word is extremely rare and archaic even by Shakespeare's day, lending her speech a deliberately elevated, almost ceremonial tone.

anchor_text: Imprimis, It is agreed between the French king
summary: 'Imprimis' (Latin: 'in the first place') is the standard opening formula of a legal document, used to introduce the first item in a list of articles or conditions. Gloucester reads the treaty aloud — a device that lets Shakespeare stage its terms for the audience and makes Gloucester's visible distress (he drops the paper) a theatrical shock.

anchor_text: the duchy of Anjou and the county of Maine shall be released
summary: Anjou and Maine were French territories the English had held since Henry V's conquests; they were the last substantial English possessions in France apart from Normandy. Surrendering them as the price of the marriage — without any dowry coming to England — was seen by Gloucester and the other lords as a catastrophic giveaway of Henry V's legacy.
detail: Holinshed reports that the secret clause ceding Anjou and Maine was hidden from Parliament and the English lords, which made it a double scandal when it leaked: not only was England giving up territory for nothing, the deal had been concealed. The historical Henry VI did surrender the provinces in 1448, after which Normandy fell rapidly (1450), and England lost virtually everything on the continent. Shakespeare telescopes the exposure: Gloucester reads the clause publicly for the first time, collapsing in theatrical horror at what he has to announce.

anchor_text: We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk
summary: Henry rewards Suffolk by elevating him from Marquess to Duke — the highest rank of English nobility below the royal family. The creation happens on stage moments after the treaty's ruinous terms are revealed, implying that the dukedom is Suffolk's payment for brokering the deal. The other lords watching this ceremony understand the insult.
detail: Historically, William de la Pole was raised to Duke of Suffolk in June 1448. Shakespeare compresses this into the opening scene to make the connection between the dishonourable treaty and Suffolk's personal profit immediate and unmistakable. Gloucester has just dropped the treaty in shock; Henry creates Suffolk a duke in the same breath. The dramatic juxtaposition is Shakespeare's, not history's.

anchor_text: did my brother Henry spend his youth
summary: Gloucester's 'brother Henry' is King Henry V, remembered as the warrior who conquered France. In lines 82-83 his 'brother Bedford' is John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford, Henry V's brother and regent of France after Henry V's death, who held the English territories together through the 1420s. Gloucester is invoking both brothers to shame the present company for squandering their sacrifice.
detail: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, was the youngest surviving son of Henry IV and therefore the youngest brother of Henry V. John, Duke of Bedford, was the middle brother who governed France as regent from 1422 until his death in 1435. Gloucester's roll-call — Henry V's military conquest, Bedford's diplomatic maintenance, his own labors on the council — builds a three-generation case for why the treaty is a betrayal of everything the house of Lancaster built in France.

anchor_text: Fatal this marriage, cancelling your fame
summary: Gloucester's four-line anaphora — four consecutive lines each beginning with a present participle ('cancelling,' 'Blotting,' 'Razing,' 'Defacing') — builds a rhetorical assault of parallel verbs of erasure. Each verb belongs to the act of destroying a written record: cancelling a contract, blotting a name from a book, razing (scraping away) characters from parchment, defacing a monument. The pattern enacts the obliteration Gloucester is describing.
detail: The figure is called 'anaphora' (Greek: repetition at the start of successive clauses) and serves as a crescendo. 'Characters' here means written letters or inscriptions, not people — 'razing the characters' means erasing the engraved praise of your deeds. Shakespeare pairs the rhetorical form with its content: the speech about erasure is itself a list of acts of erasure. Gloucester uses the same device again with 'Shall... Shall... Shall...' two lines earlier (TLN 94-96).

anchor_text: This peroration with such circumstance
summary: A 'peroration' is the formal conclusion of a speech in classical rhetoric — the section designed to stir the audience's emotions. Beaufort is mocking Gloucester for staging a theatrical harangue: 'Why the grand speech with all this elaborate circumstance [detail]?' The word signals that the Cardinal has recognized Gloucester's speech for the deliberate rhetorical performance it is — and is contemptuous of it.

anchor_text: poor King Reignier, whose large style agrees not with the leanness of his purse
summary: Reignier (Rene of Anjou, 1409-1480) held the titles King of Naples, Sicily, and Jerusalem, but never actually controlled those kingdoms — he was the 'King of Naples without a kingdom.' His 'large style' (his long string of titles) contrasted embarrassingly with his poverty and his inability to pay a dowry, which is Gloucester's scornful point: England married a pauper's daughter and gave away its own land to boot.
detail: Rene of Anjou's many nominal titles were the subject of contemporary mockery. He had claims to Naples, which he lost to Alfonso V of Aragon by 1442, and to Jerusalem as a dynastic courtesy title he never exercised. 'Style' here means the formal list of a person's titles as used in official documents. The joke — a king of three kingdoms who cannot afford to pay a dowry — was well-established by Shakespeare's time.

anchor_text: These counties were the keys of Normandy
summary: Anjou and Maine lay on the southern flank of Normandy; whoever held them could control the roads into the duchy. Salisbury's military metaphor — the two counties are 'keys' that lock or unlock Normandy — was strategically accurate: English commanders consistently argued that ceding them would make Normandy impossible to defend, as events proved when the duchy fell to the French in 1450.

anchor_text: Mort Dieu
summary: A French oath meaning 'God's death' — a minced imprecation on Christ's death on the cross. Warwick's use of French profanity here signals his long service in France and his rage: ordinary English oaths are not strong enough for what he feels. The exclamation stands alone on its line, a single outburst after twenty lines of controlled argument.

anchor_text: Suffolk should demand a whole fifteenth
summary: A 'fifteenth' was a standard form of parliamentary taxation in medieval and Tudor England: the crown would levy a tax assessed at one-fifteenth of the value of subjects' movable goods. Parliament had to grant it, which made it a constitutional measure. Suffolk demanding a full fifteenth to pay his own travel expenses in fetching the queen was seen as brazen profiteering at public expense.

anchor_text: he is the next of blood, and heir apparent to the English crown
summary: Cardinal Beaufort is reminding the lords that Gloucester, as the only surviving son of Henry IV, is heir presumptive to the childless Henry VI. Should Henry die without children, Gloucester would inherit the crown. This, Beaufort implies, is the real reason Gloucester protests the treaty: not patriotism but dynastic self-interest. The claim is itself manipulative — Beaufort uses it to turn the lords against Gloucester.
detail: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester was indeed the last surviving son of Henry IV in 1445, and if Henry VI died without heirs he was the next in the direct Lancastrian line. The Cardinal's insinuation — that Gloucester's grief over France masks a calculated attempt to preserve the kingdom he expects to inherit — is a standard piece of political slander. York, who listens silently, has his own private reasons for wanting Gloucester discredited.

anchor_text: We'll quickly hoise Duke Humphrey from his seat
summary: 'Hoise' is an older form of 'hoist' — to lift, raise, or force someone upward and then remove them. Buckingham means to lever Gloucester out of the Protectorship. The imagery of hoisting a man out of his seat is deliberately physical: the Protector will be forcibly dislodged rather than persuaded to go.

anchor_text: Unto the main! O father, Maine is lost
summary: Warwick plays on two homophone senses of 'main' across four lines: (1) 'the main' as the chief concern or principal object (Salisbury's intended meaning: 'let us attend to the main business') and (2) 'Maine,' the French province just surrendered. The joke is bitter — the moment someone says 'let's tend to the main,' Warwick hears the province he personally conquered slipping away. He then adds a third play: 'Main chance' means the safe, practical course, but to him the only 'chance' that matters is the chance to win Maine back.

summary: 'Tickle' here means precarious, unstable, easily toppled — the same sense as in 'ticklish situation.' York means that Normandy's defensive position is now desperately uncertain. The word had no comic connotation in this usage; it was a standard term for insecurity or delicacy.

anchor_text: I will take the Nevils' parts
summary: The Nevilles (here 'Nevils') were the most powerful noble family in northern England: the Earl of Salisbury and his son the Earl of Warwick, both on stage. York reveals his calculation: he will ally himself publicly with these powerful lords — men who have real armies and popular credit — as a political base from which to claim the crown when the time is right.
detail: The Neville alliance was the cornerstone of Yorkist power in the Wars of the Roses. Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, would become 'the Kingmaker' — the magnate who made and unmade kings between 1460 and 1471. York's aside shows him as a cold strategist, not merely an angry claimant: he knows he needs military and aristocratic backing before he can move openly, and he picks his allies with precision.

summary: A 'mark' is an archery target — specifically the bull's-eye or aiming point. 'The golden mark' is the crown itself, the ultimate prize York is aiming at. The metaphor of archery was common in Tudor speech for any goal aimed at deliberately.

anchor_text: Then will I raise aloft the milk-white rose, With whose sweet smell the air shall be perfum'd, And in my standard bear the arms of York
summary: The white rose was the badge of the house of York; raising it against the Lancastrian red rose is York's declaration of the coming civil war. This speech closes the scene with York's private manifesto: he will wait until Henry is distracted, then openly claim the crown with the Yorkist rose as his standard. The image crystallizes the play's role as the origin of the Wars of the Roses.
detail: The Tudor rose symbol — combining the white Yorkist rose with the red Lancastrian rose — was the dynasty's central propaganda image, and Shakespeare's audiences would have recognized both roses instantly. York's 'milk-white rose' consciously echoes the Temple-garden scene of 1 Henry VI (2.4) where lords first pluck white or red roses to choose sides. Hall's Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548) — whose very title announces the dynastic theme — and Holinshed both emphasize the rose symbolism. The whole tetralogy moves toward the union of the two roses under the first Tudor, Henry VII.

anchor_text: over-ripen'd corn, Hanging the head at Ceres' plenteous load
summary: Ceres is the Roman goddess of grain and harvest; her 'plenteous load' is the weight of ripe grain bowing the stalk. Eleanor compares Gloucester's dejected posture to a cornstalk drooping under the very abundance it has produced — he is weighed down by the prosperity and honor that should be his crowning achievement.
detail: The image is drawn from Roman pastoral imagery of Ceres as the provider of earthly abundance; Ovid's Metamorphoses 5.341-571 gives her fullest mythological treatment (Golding's 1567 translation was widely read). The simile is ironic: Gloucester should be at the height of power as Lord Protector, yet he is visibly failing under the pressure of that position. Eleanor uses a complimentary figure that is also subtly reproachful.

Ovid Metamorphoses 5.341-571 is the genuine Ceres/Proserpina passage and does present Ceres as the goddess of grain and earthly abundance; Golding's 1567 translation is a real, widely-cited English rendering.

The simile is grounded in the text (Eleanor compares Gloucester's drooping posture to a cornstalk bowing under its own harvest weight), and the characterization as simultaneously complimentary and reproachful is defensible from her rhetorical purpose of goading him.

anchor_text: King Henry's diadem, Enchas'd with all the honours of the world
summary: 'Diadem' is a crown or royal headband. 'Enchas'd' (from 'enchase') means set or embossed with jewels, as a goldsmith sets a gem into a metal mount. Eleanor is asking whether Gloucester sees in his mind's eye the royal crown, studded with the glories of kingship.
detail: The verb 'enchase' derives from Old French enchâsser, 'to set in a case or mount'; in Shakespeare it always carries the idea of jewels or ornamental work set into a surface. The diadem here is not just a crown but the full weight of royal authority. Eleanor's question is designed to probe — and stoke — Gloucester's ambition: she wants to know if he is thinking about seizing the throne.

'Enchased' as 'set with jewels' is the standard Elizabethan sense and the reading that the context — Eleanor urging Gloucester to imagine possessing the crown — supports; the detail that she is probing and stoking his ambition is clearly borne out by lines 267-276.

anchor_text: Banish the canker of ambitious thoughts
summary: 'Canker' is a spreading sore or rot, especially the kind that eats away at the interior of a plant or living thing from within. Gloucester is telling Eleanor to root out ambitious thinking the way a gardener cuts out a canker before it destroys the whole plant — a disease metaphor, not just a moral abstraction.
detail: In Elizabethan usage 'canker' covered several meanings: the eating sore (noma or gangrenous ulcer), the cankerworm that devours buds and blossoms, and wild dog-roses (called canker-roses, inferior to cultivated ones). All three senses cluster around the idea of corruption that looks healthy on the outside while devouring from within. The disease-of-ambition figure is common in Shakespeare's histories (compare Richard II's 'canker'd Bolingbroke,' Richard II 1.4).

anchor_text: this staff, mine office-badge in court, Was broke in twain
summary: The Lord Protector's white staff (a long white rod of office) was the physical emblem of his authority to govern in the king's name. A dream in which it is broken in two is a direct omen of the loss of that office. The heads of Somerset and Suffolk on the broken pieces show who Gloucester suspects will bring him down.
detail: The white staff or wand of office was the standard symbol of great household and state offices in England: the Lord Steward, the Lord Chamberlain, and the Lord Protector each held one, and its ceremonial breaking signaled the end of that office (as at a monarch's death, when the officers of the household broke their staves over the open grave). Gloucester's dream is therefore not obscure imagery but a specific, institution-grounded sign: someone will break the Protectorate. Holinshed records the political rivalry between Gloucester and his opponents at court (Chronicles, 1587).

anchor_text: Follow I must; I cannot go before While Gloster bears this base and humble mind

anchor_text: Margery Jourdain, the cunning witch, With Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer
summary: Margery Jourdain ('the Witch of Eye') and Roger Bolingbroke were real people executed in 1441 for procuring the casting of King Henry VI's horoscope on behalf of Eleanor Cobham. 'Cunning' (from 'kenning,' knowledge) applied to men and women who claimed practical magical knowledge — charms, healing, divination — and was legally distinct from full 'witchcraft,' though both were prosecuted. A conjurer claimed to summon and command spirits by ritual means. The clarification that this Bolingbroke is not Henry IV is essential: the name was common enough in the period, and the plays' audiences had just seen a Henry Bolingbroke dominating the Henriad.

anchor_text: Hume's knavery will be the duchess' wrack, And her attainture will be Humphrey's fall
summary: 'Wrack' means ruin or destruction (related to 'wreck'). 'Attainture' (also 'attainder') is the legal term for the forfeiture of civil rights, property, and social rank following a conviction for treason or felony — once 'attainted,' a person's blood was 'corrupted,' meaning their heirs could not inherit. For Eleanor, attainder would mean not only her personal ruin but the blotting of her husband's honor — which is exactly what happens. Hume speaks with the detached pragmatism of a man who has thought the whole chain through to its end and accepted that his knavery is the mechanism.

anchor_text: Against the Duke of Suffolk for enclosing the commons of Melford
summary: 'Enclosing the commons' meant a landlord fencing off common land — fields and meadows that villagers had the customary right to graze their animals on — for his own use. In Tudor England this was a bitter grievance: enclosure deprived poor communities of their livelihoods and drove people off the land. A petition against Suffolk for this offense was exactly what common people brought to the Lord Protector.
detail: Enclosure was a major social flashpoint throughout the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. When lords or wealthy farmers converted open-field arable and common pasture to private sheep-runs, smaller tenants lost the grazing rights their families had held for generations, and whole villages could be emptied. Protests and riots against enclosures (1536, 1549, 1607 and others) were recurrent. The petition against Suffolk carries the implication that the Duke's power and greed are already damaging the commons directly — a charge that will metastasize into Jack Cade's rebellion in Act 4. Long Melford is in Suffolk; the detail is locally precise.

anchor_text: the Duke of York was rightful heir to the crown
summary: York's genealogical claim to the English throne rested on descent from Edward III through both the Mortimer line (from Edward's second surviving son, Lionel of Clarence) and the York line (from his fourth son, Edmund of Langley). That senior line, the Yorks argued, outranked the Lancastrian descent from John of Gaunt (the third surviving son), making Henry VI a usurper. Peter's report of what the armorer Horner said is therefore an act of treason by any who spoke or agreed with it.

To say the king was an 'usurper' meant the crown had been illegally held since Henry Bolingbroke took it from Richard II in 1399 — every Lancastrian monarch since was thereby tainted. Shakespeare's audience, who had watched Richard II, Henry IV Part 1 and 2, and Henry V, already knew the dynastic wound; this scene begins bringing it to crisis. York publicly denies awareness of the allegation while privately pursuing the very claim Peter's master has spoken aloud.

Margaret's contemptuous ease with such language reveals her character — she has already destroyed their petitions and now dismisses the petitioners themselves with a vulgarity.

anchor_text: Is this the guise, Is this the fashion in the court of England? Is this the government of Britain's isle, And this the royalty of Albion's king

The insistent repetition mimics mounting outrage and turns each repeated phrase into an accusation. 'Albion' is a poetic, ancient name for Britain.

Margaret's four-part anaphora casts the humiliating scene with the petitioners as representative of a fundamental failure of royal governance — each 'Is this' broadening the charge from the specific incident to the constitution of the realm itself. 'Albion,' from a Celtic root perhaps meaning 'white' (the white cliffs), was the ancient Latin-poetic name for Britain, used to give formal, elevated register.

Margaret reminds Suffolk that she first noticed and admired him there, not the king she was being given to.

Holinshed records Suffolk's prominent role in the negotiations and hints at the personal admiration that arose between him and Margaret. anchor_text: To number Ave-Maries on his beads
summary: To count 'Ave Maries on his beads' is to tell a rosary — a Catholic devotional practice in which a string of beads is used to count repetitions of the Hail Mary prayer ('Ave Maria' is Latin for 'Hail Mary'). Margaret mockingly says Henry's warriors are prayers and scripture rather than soldiers and weapons — his 'tilt-yard' is his study, his weapons are biblical quotations. For an Elizabethan Protestant audience, rosary devotion was also a marker of a backward, popish piety.

It had been discouraged in Protestant England. Margaret's catalogue of Henry's 'weapons' — Ave Maries, prophets, apostles, holy saws of scripture, brazen images of saints — is a sustained mockery of a king who belongs in a monastery, not on a throne. The list also implies a structural failing in the realm: no king who fights with prayers can govern or defend a kingdom, and the power vacuum is precisely what the scene has been demonstrating.

It was the most recognizable symbol of papal power in the sixteenth century. The jab is edgier in a Protestant England where the papacy itself was a hostile foreign power — her French Catholicism makes the sneer more complex for a 1590s audience.

anchor_text: Cannot do more in England than the Nevils; Salisbury and Warwick are no simple peers
summary: The Nevilles were the most powerful noble family in northern England: the Earl of Salisbury (Richard Neville) and his son the Earl of Warwick — the future 'Kingmaker' — commanded enormous patronage, military retinues, and regional loyalty. Suffolk is warning that even he and the queen cannot outmaneuver the Neville bloc. 'No simple peers' means no ordinary or insignificant lords.

Their eventual alliance with York against the Lancastrian court was the decisive shift that opened civil war at St Albans. Suffolk's aside here establishes them as a counterweight no faction can ignore — the only lord in England who can check any single player. Shakespeare is quietly forecasting the Kingmaker's role in the plays ahead.

anchor_text: Contemptuous base-born callat as she is
summary: A 'callat' (also spelled 'callet' or 'callot') was an Elizabethan term of abuse for a woman of low or loose character — a scold, a slut, or an impudent woman of base birth. Margaret is calling Eleanor Cobham, Duchess of Gloucester, a common, uppity nobody who has forgotten her station.
detail: The insult is doubly pointed: Eleanor Cobham was indeed of lower social origin than a duchess would typically be (she was Gloucester's former mistress before he married her), and her ambitions to queenly state were notorious. Margaret's charge that Eleanor 'vaunted 'mongst her minions' about the value of her worst gown exposes the social performance of wealth by someone whose rank is newly acquired rather than hereditary. 'Base-born' targets Eleanor's origins specifically.

anchor_text: Suffolk gave two dukedoms for his daughter
summary: To obtain Margaret as Henry's bride, Suffolk agreed in the Treaty of Tours (1444) that England would surrender its claims to the French territories of Maine and Anjou — Margaret's father René's domains — as a condition of the marriage. 'Two dukedoms' refers to these lost French possessions, not literal English titles. Margaret's father, René of Anjou, was notoriously poor; the surrender of Maine and Anjou was widely resented in England as a humiliating diplomatic defeat.
detail: René of Anjou held the titles Duke of Anjou and titular King of Sicily but was largely landless in practice; the joke that he was 'king of Naples' with no actual kingdom was current. The cession of Maine was confirmed and executed in 1448, provoking enormous anger in England — it was later among the charges leveled against Suffolk when he was arrested in 1450. Margaret's own bitter awareness of this bargain gives the speech a sharp irony: she knows she was traded away for nothing, and that the queen of England is secretly mocked for coming from poor stock. For the historical context, see Holinshed.

anchor_text: myself have lim'd a bush for her, And plac'd a quire of such enticing birds
summary: Suffolk uses birdliming as a metaphor for his trap against Eleanor. Birdlime was a sticky substance spread on branches to catch small birds by their feet. Suffolk has 'limed a bush' — set a sticky trap — and placed a 'quire' (a group, literally a choir) of tempting birds who will sing to Eleanor until she lands and cannot escape. This is how he plans to destroy the Duchess.
detail: Birdlime was made from holly bark or mistletoe berries and daubed on twigs; a bird landing on the branch would be held fast by the glue. The practice was common enough to be a recognized metaphor for any sticky entrapment. The 'enticing birds' are almost certainly the corrupt priest John Hume and others who are cultivating Eleanor's ambitions (her desire to use witchcraft to foresee the king's death) while secretly working for Suffolk and the Cardinal. In 1.2 we have already seen Hume confess to exactly this double game. Suffolk's tone is that of a confident schemer — he has the trap set, and the Duchess is about to spring it.

anchor_text: Since thou wert king--as who is king but thou?--
summary: Suffolk's parenthetical aside — 'as who is king but thou?' — is the scene's sharpest accusation: Gloucester, as Lord Protector, has wielded kingly power while the nominal king Henry VI has been a passive cipher. The dash-framed question cuts deeper than the surrounding charges of poor governance because it questions the constitutional legitimacy of the entire Protectorship.
detail: The Lord Protector's office was created for Gloucester to govern during Henry's minority; Henry is now technically old enough to rule in his own right, which is precisely why Margaret has been asking why the Protector is still needed (lines 481-484). Suffolk's taunt identifies a genuine political problem: a realm with two sovereign authorities — the anointed king and the man who effectively runs it — is a realm with a fractured body politic. The jibe supports the play's larger interest in the 'king's two bodies': what happens to the body politic when the body natural of the king cannot govern?

anchor_text: Could I come near your beauty with my nails, I'd set my ten commandments in your face
summary: Eleanor's 'ten commandments' are her ten fingernails — the joke being that a woman's scratching claws are her law. The phrase was a common colloquial expression in Elizabethan English for the fingers (each nail a 'commandment' to be obeyed). Eleanor is threatening to scratch Margaret's face raw.
detail: The colloquialism equating ten fingernails with the Ten Commandments was sufficiently common for contemporaries to recognize it as a proverbial jest. It implies a distinctly unqueenly, brawling mode of women's violence — scratching rather than fighting with weapons. The double meaning gives Eleanor's fury a comic edge even as it escalates the confrontation: she is so enraged that she has to be restrained by convention and royal presence, and the code-violation of Margaret's unprovoked slap has just removed that restraint. The biblical echo (Exodus 20) is entirely ironic — Eleanor is invoking a code of law and divine order while threatening physical assault.

The 'ten commandments = ten fingernails' colloquialism is well-attested via Onions and Tilley C525, and the biblical irony is correctly characterized as incidental rather than the primary meaning.

anchor_text: She's tickled now; her fume needs no spurs, She'll gallop far enough to her destruction
summary: Buckingham mixes two images: Eleanor is 'tickled' (provoked, irritated into reckless motion) and her anger ('fume') is a horse that 'needs no spurs' — no additional goading — before it 'gallops' her straight to ruin. The extended horse-riding metaphor turns Eleanor's rage into a runaway animal that will carry its rider to disaster without any further push from her enemies.
detail: The metaphor is precise and cynical: Buckingham is confirming that the trap (the 'limed bush' Suffolk described) is sprung. The public humiliation from Margaret's slap has inflamed Eleanor to precisely the rash, resentful behaviour that will make her easy prey for the conjurors Hume has placed in her path. 'Fume' means both anger and the vapour of passion thought to rise from the blood to the brain and cloud judgment — in Galenic medicine the humour of choler produced both heat and rash action. The line tells the audience that Eleanor's fall is now inevitable from her own character, not merely from her enemies' conspiracy.

anchor_text: Without discharge, money, or furniture
summary: 'Discharge' here means release from service or dismissal from duty — York fears he will be sent to France as regent but never formally recalled or paid off. 'Furniture' means military equipment and supplies — the arms, horses, provisions, and materiel needed to run a campaign. York's complaint is that Somerset will keep him tied to France without releasing him and without sending him the resources to actually succeed there.
detail: York is recalling what happened 'last time' (line 536): he commanded in France, was denied reinforcements and money, and Paris fell. Now he fears the same scenario: appointed regent but deliberately starved of resources so that his failure can be attributed to him, not to Somerset's deliberate obstruction. 'Furniture' as military equipment (cf. 'furniture of war') was standard sixteenth-century usage; the complaint about 'discharge' points to the military law obligation to formally release an officer from his command before he could leave his post — without it York would be stranded. This is the specific grievance that will curdle into York's decision to take the throne by force.

anchor_text: Base dunghill villain and mechanical
summary: York calls Peter a 'mechanical' — that is, a manual laborer, a craftsman, someone who works with his hands for wages. In the social hierarchy of Shakespeare's England, 'mechanicals' were the artisan class below the gentry; calling someone a 'mechanical' was a contemptuous class insult, grouping them with the tradesmen and servants who had no standing to accuse their betters.
detail: The word comes from Latin 'mechanicus,' pertaining to manual work, and in Elizabethan English acquired the contemptuous meaning 'of the artisan class, base, vulgar.' The term is used the same way in A Midsummer Night's Dream, where the craftsmen who perform the interlude are called 'rude mechanicals' (3.2). York's fury at being accused of treason by an armorer's apprentice — a man of the lowest social rung who had no right to speak against a duke — is partly class outrage: the accusation is as degrading as its source.

The class-insult sense of 'mechanical' (manual laborer, artisan, below the gentry) is accurate; the MSND parallel to 'rude mechanicals' is correct and illuminating.

anchor_text: This doom, my lord, if I may judge: Let Somerset be Regent o'er the French, Because in York this breeds suspicion; And let these have a day appointed them For single combat in convenient place
summary: Gloucester's 'doom' (judgment, legal ruling) resolves the crisis by two separate decisions: make Somerset regent so that York is not compromised by the treason charge while his own man is accused, and settle the accusation between Horner and Peter by 'single combat' — a judicial duel. Trial by combat was an ancient legal remedy for treason accusations when there was no other evidence: God would grant victory to whichever side told the truth.
detail: The belief underlying trial by combat was that divine providence would not allow the guilty party to win; it was therefore a form of ordeal rather than merely a test of strength. In practice an armorer fighting his own apprentice would be expected to win easily — a master trained in arms against an untrained boy. The duel takes place in 2.3, and Horner loses, dying and confessing. Gloucester's use of the procedure reflects his reputation as a strict but honest judge who respects old law even when it disadvantages his political allies: by setting the combat, he effectively clears the path for Somerset's appointment while leaving the treason charge against York unresolved. The card on trial by combat in the reference file covers this specific case as well as Richard II's aborted duel.

anchor_text: hear our exorcisms
summary: 'Exorcisms' here does not mean casting out a demon but rather summoning one up — the word could cover both the conjuring and the dismissal of spirits in Elizabethan usage. Roger Bolingbroke is asking whether Eleanor is prepared to witness the conjuring ceremony.
detail: The modern sense (expelling an evil spirit) and the older sense (compelling a spirit to appear and answer) both descend from Latin exorcizare, 'to bind by oath.' In early modern English both meanings coexisted; context here makes clear that the rite summons rather than banishes. The scene stages the historical 1441 conjuring of Roger Bolingbroke and Margery Jourdain at the behest of Eleanor Cobham, Duchess of Gloucester.

anchor_text: The time of night when Troy was set on fire
summary: Troy, the legendary city of Asia Minor, was sacked and burned by the Greeks after a ten-year siege; in the classical tradition the wooden horse allowed Greek warriors inside the walls at night, and the slaughter and burning began in darkness. Bolingbroke invokes the destruction of Troy as the archetype of catastrophe unfolding under cover of night, to build an atmosphere of supernatural dread.
detail: The fall of Troy was the most famous catastrophe in classical memory. Virgil's Aeneid 2 describes the sack in detail, including the darkness and the fires that consumed the city. Ovid, Marlowe, and the broader literary tradition made the night-time burning of Troy a standard emblem of total destruction. Bolingbroke's incantation works atmospherically: night, silence, owl-cries, restless spirits, and Troy's fires together construct the ideal moment for raising the dead.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 601

Bolingbroke's incantation is building atmospheric catalogue of ominous nocturnal signs (silence, screech-owls, ban-dogs, restless spirits), and the sack of Troy as the archetype of catastrophe-by-night fits squarely within that rhetorical register; the Aeneid 2 anchor is appropriate.

anchor_text: Adsum
summary: 'Adsum' is Latin for 'I am here' or 'present' — the demon announcing its arrival at Jourdain's call. The Latin formula is deliberate: ceremonial conjuring used Latin throughout, so the spirit's first word places it squarely within the ritual language of learned demonology rather than folk magic.
detail: Latin was the language of the Church, of scholarship, and — by extension — of high-register ritual, including conjuring as depicted in Renaissance demonology. The spirit answers in Latin, then shifts to English for its prophecies; the contrast marks a transition from formal compulsion to actual communication. 'Asmath' (spelled 'Asnath' in some editions) is the spirit's proper name as it is addressed; the name does not correspond to any canonical demon name in the standard demonological catalogues, and is probably a theatrical coinage or textual corruption.

The annotation is sound: 'Adsum' is straightforwardly Latin for 'I am here/present,' the spirit does then shift to English for its answers, and the candid acknowledgment that 'Asnath/Asmath' is not a canonical demon name and is likely a theatrical coinage is appropriately honest rather than over-claiming.

anchor_text: The duke yet lives that Henry shall depose, But him outlive and die a violent death
summary: The spirit's first prophecy is a deliberately riddling double-meaning: it can be read as 'the duke who will depose Henry still lives' (pointing to York) or as 'Henry will depose some duke' (pointing to Gloucester). York reads it the first way; Eleanor hopes for the first way too. The prophecy is designed to be true whichever way it falls — a trick of oracle-craft known as amphibology.
detail: Amphibology (deliberate grammatical ambiguity) is the classic mark of oracular speech from Delphi onward; a riddling prophecy cannot be falsified because it can always be made to fit events after the fact. The spirit's answer hedges in both directions: the subject of 'shall depose' is syntactically unclear, and 'him' in the second line refers back to the ambiguous subject of the first. York, reading the written text in lines 644-647, draws a parallel to the most famous ambiguous oracle of antiquity. Shakespeare's Holinshed source records that the real prophecy cast for Eleanor in 1441 dealt with the King's horoscope; the play sharpens it into a triple set of riddles (Henry, Suffolk, Somerset) whose ironic fulfilment the later acts pay off.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the conjuring and prophecies of Roger Bolingbroke at the Duchess of Gloucester's direction, 1441.

The amphibology reading is defensible — York himself signals it by comparing the prophecy to the Pyrrhus oracle — but the gloss goes further than the text strictly requires by asserting Eleanor 'hopes for the first way too,' which the text does not show at this moment (she is arrested before she can react); the core identification of deliberate syntactic ambiguity is sound, but the Eleanor-interpretation claim is an interpolation.

anchor_text: Descend to darkness and the burning lake! False fiend, avoid
summary: The 'burning lake' is hell — specifically the lake of fire described in Revelation as the final destination of Satan and the damned. Bolingbroke dismisses the spirit back to the infernal regions with a formula that blends demonological convention and biblical imagery. 'Avoid' here means 'be gone' or 'depart,' not 'be careful.'
detail: The 'lake of fire' appears in Revelation 19:20 and 20:10, 14-15 as the second death, into which the Beast, the False Prophet, and eventually Satan are cast. It was the standard Protestant-era mental picture of hell, and 'burning lake' became a set phrase for the infernal pit. Milton's Satan finds himself in a 'burning lake' in Paradise Lost 1.210-11 — the same cultural fixture. Dismissal formulas — ordering the spirit back to darkness after it has given its answers — were expected parts of the conjuring convention and are staged here with the thunder and lightning of the stage direction that follows.

anchor_text: Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse
summary: This is the most famous ambiguous oracle of antiquity, quoted in Latin: 'I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can defeat the Romans' — or equally, 'the Romans can defeat you.' The oracle was given to Pyrrhus of Epirus before his campaign against Rome (c. 280 BCE); it was true whichever side won. York uses it to mark the spirit's prophecy about Henry as equally double-edged: it cannot be pinned down to a single meaning.
detail: The oracle is quoted by Cicero (De Divinatione 2.116) and by Ennius (in a now-fragmentary Latin original). Pyrrhus, king of Epirus and descendant of Achilles (through the Aeacid line), asked the oracle at Dodona or Delphi before invading Italy; he received this deliberately ambiguous Latin hexameter, whose subject and object can be read either way because Latin word order does not fix them. Pyrrhus interpreted it favorably, invaded, won two bloody victories ('Pyrrhic victories'), and was eventually beaten. The anecdote was a schoolroom staple — Cicero's De Divinatione was read in Tudor grammar schools — and stood as the textbook example of oracular double-speak. York's citation shows his sharp intelligence: he sees at once that the spirit's prophecy (lines 615-616) is constructed exactly this way.

The oracle's source in Cicero's De Divinatione, the Pyrrhus context, the syntactic ambiguity of Latin word-order, and York's use of it to gloss the spirit's riddling prophecy are all accurate and well within the mainstream scholarly and schoolroom tradition.

anchor_text: These oracles are hardly attain'd, And hardly understood
summary: York uses 'hardly' twice with a deliberate double sense: the first means 'obtained with difficulty' (hard to get), the second 'scarcely' or 'with difficulty' (hard to read). The repetition also carries a third meaning lurking under both: 'harsh' or 'severe' — oracles won by dark arts and pointing to violent fates. The pun is tight and York delivers it drily.
detail: In Elizabethan English 'hardly' could mean (1) 'with difficulty' (from 'hard' = difficult), (2) 'scarcely, barely,' and (3) 'harshly, severely' — all three senses related to the stem 'hard.' York's first use ('hardly attain'd') draws on sense 1: summoning a demon through thunder and treasonable conjuring is no easy business. The second ('hardly understood') draws on sense 2: these riddling prophecies, once obtained, are almost impossible to decode with certainty. The ambient harshness of what they foretell (violent deaths, castle-traps, drowning) quietly activates sense 3 as well. The compressed wit is characteristic of York's detached, calculating intelligence — he can appreciate the craft of a treason even as he seizes its evidence.

The primary two senses of 'hardly' (with difficulty / scarcely) are clearly operative in the repeated word, but the claim that a third sense 'harshly/severely' is also actively meant as a third layer is speculative — the word in both instances fits sense 1 and 2 cleanly, and positing a three-way pun where two senses already fully account for the usage risks over-reading; the core double-sense observation is sound.

anchor_text: flying at the brook
summary: Falconry phrase: 'flying at the brook' means flying hawks at waterfowl along a stream or marsh, a form of hawking done with falcons trained to strike birds in flight over water. The court is at St Albans on a royal hunting excursion.
detail: Elizabethan hawking was a major aristocratic pastime. 'The brook' was the watercourse the falconers 'beat' to flush water-birds; the falcon then 'towers' overhead waiting to strike. The vocabulary of the sport — 'pitch' (the height the falcon climbs), 'tower' (to wheel high), 'put up the fowl' (to flush it) — runs through the scene's first forty lines and is then systematically turned into political metaphor by Suffolk and Gloucester.

anchor_text: what a pitch she flew above the rest
summary: 'Pitch' is a falconry term for the highest point a hawk rises before stooping (diving) to strike its quarry. Henry's innocent remark about Gloucester's falcon flying highest will be picked up immediately by Suffolk as a malicious gibe about Gloucester's political ambitions.
detail: Bert's Approved Treatise defines 'pitch' as the height a hawk gains while 'towering' — its greatest elevation before the stoop. The pun is established by Henry's innocent usage and then exploited: Suffolk's 'bears his thoughts above his falcon's pitch' (TLN 680) converts the same word into an accusation that Gloucester aims above his station. The transit from sport to politics in these thirty lines is the play's first piece of compressed allegory.

anchor_text: Tantaene animis coelestibus irae
summary: Gloucester quotes Latin from the opening of Virgil's Aeneid: 'Can such anger dwell in heavenly minds?' (Aeneid 1.11). He turns the epic's lament that a goddess would stoop to such petty rage into a taunt at the Cardinal — a churchman acting with passion unbecoming a man of God.
detail: Virgil's first book opens by asking why Juno persecuted the pious Aeneas: 'Tantaene animis coelestibus irae?' (Aen. 1.11). Gloucester's quotation is deliberately precise and witty: the 'coelestibus' ('heavenly') lands with extra irony on the Cardinal, who is supposed to represent the heavenly realm. A grammar-school education in Elizabethan England meant reading Virgil in Latin; quoting the Aeneid was a standard display of classical authority. The line also caps Gloucester's jibe at TLN 685 ('Were it not good your grace could fly to heaven?') — the Cardinal's 'heaven,' it is implied, is earthly ambition.

anchor_text: blessed are the peacemakers on earth
summary: Henry quotes the Beatitudes from the Sermon on the Mount: 'Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God' (Matthew 5:9). The verse is characteristic of Henry's reflexive piety; the Cardinal immediately and wickedly volunteers himself as a peacemaker — against Gloucester, with his sword.
detail: The Beatitudes are the eight blessings Jesus pronounces in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3-12, Geneva 1599). Henry's instinct is always to reach for scripture when confronted by conflict, and this is his defining gesture across the Henry VI plays: godly, passive, and politically helpless. The Cardinal's instant twisting of the text ('Let me be blessed for the peace I make / Against this proud protector, with my sword!' TLN 705-706) is a sharp emblem of how the court uses religion as cover for faction.

anchor_text: I'll shave your crown for this
summary: Gloucester's threat contains a pun: 'crown' means both the top of the Cardinal's tonsured head (which Gloucester threatens to cut) and his dignity or rank. 'Shave your crown' literally threatens a close blade to the head, but the secondary meaning strips the Cardinal of his clerical status and his lordly 'crown' in one gesture.
detail: A priest's tonsure — the shaved patch on the crown of the head — was the outward sign of clerical status. Gloucester's threat to 'shave your crown' therefore works on two levels: he will wound the Cardinal in the impending duel (cutting him on the top of his head) and he will 'shave' — in the sense of scrape away or strip — the Cardinal's dignity. 'Or all my fence shall fail' confirms this is a fencing challenge: 'fence' = the art of sword-play (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fence').

anchor_text: a blind man at Saint Alban's shrine
summary: St Alban was Britain's first Christian martyr, executed around 304 CE; his shrine at the town bearing his name was a major pilgrimage destination in medieval England, credited with miraculous healings. Blind men, the lame, and the sick traveled there seeking cures, making the scene of a miraculous cure entirely plausible to the crowd, and providing Gloucester a ready-made fraud to expose.
detail: St Alban was a Romano-British soldier martyred under Diocletian; his cult centered on the abbey at Verulamium (St Albans, Hertfordshire). Pilgrimages to saints' shrines and claims of miraculous healing at them were common throughout the medieval period, and though the Reformation had officially suppressed the cult of relics and pilgrimage by the 1540s, popular credulity about miracle-sites persisted. Simpcox's story — called there by the saint in repeated dreams, healed of blindness — was a standard format for reported shrine-miracles, which is exactly what makes the fraud so shameless: he knows the formula that devout people will believe.

anchor_text: Born blind, an 't please your grace
summary: Simpcox's claim to have been born blind and miraculously cured echoes the New Testament story of the man born blind healed by Jesus at Siloam (John 9:1-7), which was the most famous biblical precedent for this exact type of miracle. Henry, who is steeped in scripture, immediately credits the cure. Gloucester's exposure of the fraud implicitly casts him as the skeptic testing a claim that pious Henry would never question.
detail: John 9 is the gospel account of Jesus healing a man blind from birth by making clay from spittle and earth and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam — the key distinction from other healings being that this man had never seen at all, not that he had lost his sight. The same distinction drives Gloucester's cross-examination: a man born blind could not suddenly name colors he had never seen. The biblical parallel also gives Henry's trust its logic — a man blind from birth miraculously cured is a gospel-grade miracle; Henry 'Now God be prais'd' (TLN 744) responds as a pious Christian hearing scripture fulfilled.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 756

The echo of John 9 is the obvious and mainstream reference for a congenital blindness miracle in this Christian dramatic context, and the note that Henry's credulous response follows logically from the biblical precedent is sound.

anchor_text: Mass, thou lov'dst plums well
summary: 'Mass' is a mild oath, a weakened form of 'by the Mass' — the Catholic eucharist — used as a colloquial exclamation, equivalent to 'indeed' or 'well then.' Gloucester uses it drily as he closes the trap on Simpcox: a blind man who loves plums enough to risk his life climbing for them.

anchor_text: beadles in your town, and things called whips
summary: A beadle was a parish or town officer whose duties included administering public corporal punishment — specifically, the whipping of vagabonds, petty criminals, and impostors through the streets. Whipping was the standard legal punishment for fraud and vagrancy in Tudor England. Gloucester's dry tone ('things called whips') underlines the obviousness of the remedy.
detail: Under the Elizabethan Poor Laws, vagabonds and able-bodied beggars could be stripped to the waist and whipped at the cart's tail through the streets of every town they passed through until they reached their home parish. Fraudulent miracle-claimants fell squarely in this category. The spectacle of Simpcox leaping over the stool and running — revealed as a fraud and a perfectly mobile man the moment pain threatens — is a piece of broad comic theater that serves a serious point about credulity and the ease of deceiving the credulous.

anchor_text: Duke Humphrey has done a miracle to-day
summary: The Cardinal's remark is bitter irony: Gloucester did perform a kind of secular 'miracle' — making the lame man walk, the opposite of the fraud's fake cure. Suffolk extends it: Gloucester 'made the lame to leap.' Gloucester answers with a sharper counter-irony: the Cardinal and Suffolk themselves have done 'more miracles' by making 'whole towns fly' — a jab at Suffolk's role in surrendering English territories in France.
detail: The exchange turns the language of religious miracle (healing the lame, sight to the blind) into a vehicle for political attack. Gloucester's riposte — 'You made in a day, my lord, whole towns to fly' (TLN 840) — refers to Suffolk's negotiation of the peace treaty with France that ceded Maine and Anjou (dramatized in 1 Henry VI and the opening of 2 Henry VI), a surrender widely blamed on Suffolk and deeply unpopular with the English commons. The mock-miracle language is therefore not merely witty; it is a public accusation of political catastrophe.

The ironic inversion of miracle-language is explicit in the text, and Gloucester's counter-thrust at Suffolk over the cession of Maine and Anjou is the natural and mainstream reading of 'towns to fly.'

anchor_text: A sort of naughty persons, lewdly bent
summary: 'Sort' here means 'company' or 'group' of people, not a type or category. 'Naughty' means wicked, morally bad — much stronger than its modern mild sense. 'Lewdly bent' means inclined toward wickedness or low crimes. Buckingham is reporting a conspiracy, not describing misbehaving children.

anchor_text: Dealing with witches and with conjurers
summary: Buckingham reports what the audience saw in Act 1, Scene 4: Eleanor Cobham hired a conjurer and a witch to raise a spirit and ask it the fate of the King. Using magic to foretell a monarch's death counted as high treason in Tudor law, because the prophecy could be taken as an incitement to hasten it. The historical Eleanor Cobham was convicted on exactly this charge in 1441.
detail: The Elizabethan Witchcraft Act of 1563 (5 Eliz. c. 16) made conjuring and divination for treasonable purposes a capital crime; a stronger act followed in 1604. The historical case of Eleanor Cobham's arrest for necromancy and horoscope-casting (1441) is Shakespeare's source, as reported in Holinshed. The conjurer in the play, Roger Bolingbroke, is the historical Roger Bolingbroke, a real person executed for this conspiracy — and is unrelated to the King Henry Bolingbroke (Henry IV) of the earlier history plays despite the shared surname.

The metaphor is brutal: the Cardinal is rubbing Gloucester's face in his wife's disgrace at the moment Gloucester has just learned of it.

The word 'forthcoming' (TLN 856) means 'in custody, ready for trial'; it is a legal term. The Cardinal's vindictiveness here signals how completely the political game has moved against Gloucester.

anchor_text: like to pitch defile nobility
summary: Gloucester uses the proverb 'he that touches pitch shall be defiled' — meaning that association with the base or wicked corrupts the noble, just as the sticky black tar ('pitch') stains anything it touches. The same proverbial image appears in Ecclesiasticus and in several other Shakespeare plays.
detail: The pitch-defilement proverb descends from the Apocryphal Ecclesiasticus (Sirach 13:1, Geneva 1599: 'He that toucheth pitch, shall be defiled with it: and he that is familiar with a proud man, shall be like unto him'). It was a school commonplace and appears in Benedict's mouth in Much Ado About Nothing (3.3) and in the title-character's meditations in Henry IV Part 1. Here Gloucester uses it to express genuine moral anguish: if Eleanor has 'convers'd with such / As like to pitch defile nobility,' she has contaminated the Gloucester name, and he must repudiate her — which he does with the formal legal phrase 'I banish her my bed and company' (TLN 874).

anchor_text: poise the cause in justice' equal scales
summary: 'Poise' means to weigh or balance. Henry will 'weigh the case in justice's even scales' — the scales of justice being the standard ancient emblem of impartial judgment. The closing couplet presents Henry as ideally impartial, but the audience knows Eleanor's enemies are already controlling the outcome.

Henry's confident claim that impartial justice will prevail is ironic in context: the Cardinal, Suffolk, and Margaret — who have engineered Eleanor's arrest — are standing in the same room as he makes the vow. 'Whose beam stands sure, whose rightful cause prevails' closes the scene on Henry's faith in divine justice, faith the play will methodically dismantle as Gloucester's fall proceeds.

anchor_text: if thy claim be good, The Nevils are thy subjects to command
summary: Warwick's declaration that 'the Nevils' are York's to command names the family to which both Warwick and his father Salisbury belong: the Nevilles, one of the most powerful noble houses in England. Warwick — Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, known later to history as 'the Kingmaker' — is pledging the whole network of Neville power to York's dynastic cause. This private garden meeting is where the Yorkist coalition is secretly formed.
detail: The Nevilles controlled vast estates in the north of England and could field formidable retinues. Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick (c. 1428-1471) would become the dominant military and political power of the next two decades, making and unmaking kings; his nickname 'the Kingmaker' reflects the role he begins to play here. His support for York is the turning point that makes the Yorkist challenge viable. The scene sets up the alliance that will culminate in the first battle of St Albans (Act 5) and continue through 3 Henry VI.

The identification of 'the Nevils' as the Neville family and Warwick's pledge as the founding moment of the Yorkist coalition is accurate and mainstream; the summary and detail correctly identifies this as Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, and his later 'Kingmaker' reputation is historically grounded, though the note appropriately frames it as prospective rather than present.

anchor_text: Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons
summary: York's entire claim to the crown rests on the family tree of Edward III (reigned 1327-1377), who had seven sons. The crucial argument is about birth order: Richard II, heir of the eldest son (the Black Prince), was deposed by Henry Bolingbroke, heir of the fourth son, John of Gaunt. York argues that the senior claim passed through the third son, Lionel Duke of Clarence, via the Mortimer line — making him, not King Henry VI, the rightful king. Shakespeare uses Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) as his source for this genealogy.
detail: The sons York names: (1) Edward the Black Prince, (2) William of Hatfield, (3) Lionel Duke of Clarence, (4) John of Gaunt, (5) Edmund of Langley (York's own ancestor), (6) Thomas of Woodstock, (7) William of Windsor. York's claim runs: Lionel's daughter Philippe married Edmund Mortimer Earl of March; their son Roger had a daughter Anne; Anne married Richard Earl of Cambridge (York's father, himself son of Edmund of Langley, the fifth son). So York descends on his mother's side from the third son and on his father's side from the fifth — he argues that the Clarence line is senior to Lancaster's Gaunt line, giving him a better title than Henry VI. This is the genealogy that drives the entire Wars of the Roses.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587); the descent of the sons of King Edward III.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 892

Holinshed (1587) is the genuine source for York's genealogical claim and Edward III's sons; the detail section has William of Windsor and Thomas of Woodstock swapped in birth order (Windsor was 6th, Woodstock 7th), but this is a minor prose error and does not impugn the source, which genuinely supports the core claim.

The genealogical summary accurately reflects the dynastic argument York makes in the scene, the seven sons are correctly listed in order, and the Holinshed attribution for this lineage is the standard scholarly consensus.

anchor_text: Henry Bolingbroke, Duke of Lancaster
summary: This Henry Bolingbroke is the usurping king who deposed Richard II and became Henry IV — founder of the Lancastrian royal line. He is not to be confused with Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer who raised spirits for the Duchess of Gloucester in Act 1.4 of this play. York is telling how Lancaster illegitimately seized the crown by force: Bolingbroke 'seiz'd on the realm, depos'd the rightful king,' sent Richard's queen back to France, and had Richard murdered at Pomfret Castle.
detail: Holinshed's account of Richard II's deposition (1399) and death at Pomfret (Pontefract) Castle in Yorkshire is the basis for York's summary here. Bolingbroke's claim was the central wound in the Lancastrian title: he was a younger son's heir (John of Gaunt, fourth son of Edward III), and the crown passed through him by force rather than strict hereditary right. York's recitation of this history is partly legal argument, partly propaganda — reframing the Lancastrian succession as theft.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the deposition of Richard II, 1399, and his death at Pomfret Castle.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 903
Holinshed (1587) covers Bolingbroke's deposition of Richard II in 1399 and Richard's death at Pomfret (Pontefract) Castle; the source is real and fully supports the summary.

The identification of Bolingbroke as Henry IV and the note distinguishing him from Roger Bolingbroke (the conjurer of 1.4) is a useful and accurate clarification; the characterization of York's speech as legal argument and propaganda is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: him to Pomfret, where, as all you know, Harmless Richard was murther'd traitorously
summary: Pomfret is the medieval English name for Pontefract, a castle in Yorkshire where Richard II was imprisoned after his forced abdication in 1399 and where he died that same year — almost certainly murdered, though the precise manner is uncertain. Shakespeare consistently treats the death as a deliberate murder orchestrated by Bolingbroke. 'Harmless' here means innocent or inoffensive, reinforcing York's picture of Richard as a victim rather than a threat.

The gloss on 'Pomfret' as Pontefract is correct; 'harmless' meaning innocent or inoffensive is well attested; and noting that the manner of Richard's death is uncertain while Shakespeare treats it as deliberate murder is an accurate and appropriately hedged reading.

anchor_text: fair slips of such a stock
summary: A 'slip' is a young shoot or cutting taken from a plant to be transplanted; a 'stock' is the parent stem or trunk from which a plant grows. Warwick uses horticultural language to compliment York's sons: they are vigorous young growths from a noble lineage. The plant metaphor for dynastic descent — the royal 'family tree,' with its grafts, roots, and branches — runs throughout the history plays. Here it quietly answers York's genealogical proof: Lionel's claim 'flourishes in thee / And in thy sons.'

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 941

The horticultural senses of 'slip' (cutting) and 'stock' (parent stem) are confirmed in Shakespeare's period, including in his own Winter's Tale and 2 Henry VI; specific OED sense numbers (slip 3b, stock 16) cannot be verified without direct OED access but the underlying lexical claims are accurate.

The horticultural glosses for 'slip' (cutting for transplanting) and 'stock' (parent stem) are accurate and well attested; connecting the plant metaphor to dynastic lineage is standard and mainstream, not an overreach.

anchor_text: in this private plot be we the first That shall salute our rightful sovereign
summary: The word 'plot' carries a pun: its primary sense here is a 'plot of ground,' a piece of land — they are literally standing in York's garden. But 'plot' also meant a secret scheme or conspiracy, which is exactly what they are engaged in. The pun is pointed: this garden 'plot' is also a political plot against the crown. The scene echoes the garden scene of Richard II (3.4), where the garden is an explicit allegory for the state.
detail: The overlap between 'a piece of ground' and 'a scheme or plan' was fully established in Shakespeare's English (OED s.v. 'plot,' senses 3 and 5; the conspiratorial sense is well attested from the 1580s). The stage direction places the scene in a garden, which makes the first sense literal and the second ironic: the conspirators meet on York's private turf to lay out a political conspiracy. The garden-as-kingdom metaphor runs through the second tetralogy — most explicitly in Richard II 3.4 ('Why should we, in the compass of a pale, / Keep law and form and due proportion, / Showing as in a model our firm estate?') — and York's garden repeats that symbolic register for the new cycle of usurpation.

sources.name: OED

York applies it to Gloucester, calling him the realm's true protector against the predatory courtiers around the king. The irony is deliberate: York himself is plotting to seize the throne, and is content to see the 'shepherd' destroyed because it serves his ambition.

anchor_text: by God's book are adjudg'd to death
summary: 'God's book' is the Bible. Henry is pronouncing that Eleanor and her confederates' crimes — treasonable necromancy and witchcraft — are capital offenses both under statute law and under Scripture (Leviticus 20:27 and Exodus 22:18 condemn those who consult spirits or practice sorcery). anchor_text: witch in Smithfield shall be burn'd to ashes
summary: Smithfield was a large open ground just outside London's walls, the traditional site of public executions by burning; it was where heretics and those convicted of witchcraft were put to death. Burning alive was the prescribed punishment for women convicted of petty treason (killing one's husband, counterfeiting coin) and, by assimilation, for witchcraft treated as treason. Holinshed confirms that Margery Jourdain was burned at Smithfield for her role in the Eleanor Cobham affair in 1441.

anchor_text: three days' open penance done
summary: Public penance required the condemned person to walk through the streets, usually barefoot and in a white penitential sheet, carrying a lighted taper, while a town crier announced their crime. Eleanor Cobham underwent this ritual for three days through the streets of London in 1441 — one of the most spectacular public humiliations of a great noble in English medieval history. The next scene (2.4) stages this penance.
detail: The ceremony of 'open' or 'public' penance was an ecclesiastical punishment for serious moral or spiritual offenses, administered through the Church courts. For a duchess to walk barefoot through London streets in a sheet while the commons stared was an almost unprecedented public spectacle; Holinshed stresses the crowd of witnesses. Shakespeare will stage the penance in 2.4, where a weeping Gloucester watches from a distance, unable to help his wife. The historical Eleanor's penance took place on three specific market days in November 1441.

The three-day barefoot public-penance ceremony for Eleanor Cobham is confirmed by Holinshed and Hall, and the description of the ecclesiastical form (white sheet, taper) is standard; the annotation's claim that 2.4 will stage it is accurate.

anchor_text: Give up thy staff; Henry will to himself Protector be
summary: The Lord Protector's staff of office was his emblem of authority, carried as a physical symbol of the regent's power over the realm during the king's minority. When Henry demands the staff and declares he will be his own Protector, it marks the formal end of Gloucester's regency. 'Protector' was the official title of whoever governed England on behalf of the king when the king was too young or incapacitated to rule.
detail: Gloucester had served as Lord Protector — effectively the regent who conducted royal government — from Henry VI's accession in 1422 through the king's minority. Henry's decision to govern personally and without a Protector was overdue by the 1440s (he had been king since infancy), but in the play's logic it arrives just as Eleanor's disgrace has weakened Gloucester's position, enabling his enemies to accelerate his fall. The surrendering of the staff is a stage action with real legal force: it undoes a grant of authority originally given by Henry V on his deathbed.

The staff as the Lord Protector's physical emblem of office and the scene's legal force as a formal revocation of the regency are sound; calling the moment 'overdue by the 1440s' is a reasonable and uncontroversial historical simplification.

anchor_text: lantern to my feet
summary: Henry is echoing Psalm 119:105 — 'Thy word is a lantern unto my feet, and a light unto my path' — casting God and Scripture as his guide now that he governs alone without Gloucester's counsel. The image is a direct signal of Henry's piety and also of his political inexperience: where a king might invoke strategic wisdom, Henry invokes Scripture.

Psalm 119:105 is the direct and obvious source for 'lantern to my feet,' and the standard reading that Henry's scriptural substitution for statecraft signals his piety and political naivety is mainstream scholarly opinion.

anchor_text: Thus droops this lofty pine and hangs his sprays
summary: Suffolk uses an extended plant metaphor — a tall pine tree bowed down, its branches ('sprays') hanging — to describe Gloucester's fall. The image works doubly: the 'lofty pine' is Gloucester, once the highest in the realm, and 'Eleanor's pride' is compared to a plant that dies young. The comparison of a great noble to a tall tree being felled was a standard Elizabethan figure for the fall of princes.

Suffolk's aside is gloating rather than elegiac — 'thus droops' is contemptuous pleasure. The Elizabethan idea of 'degree' (rank as a fixed hierarchy) makes the toppling of the tallest element especially resonant, since the tree's height represented both Gloucester's dignity and, in Suffolk's reading, his dangerous elevation above others. The double observation — Gloucester humbled AND Eleanor's youth cut short — packs two satisfactions into two couplet lines.

anchor_text: appellant and defendant, The armourer and his man, to enter the lists
summary: In a judicial combat, the 'appellant' is the person who makes the accusation (here Peter, the apprentice) and the 'defendant' is the one who must disprove it (here Horner, the armourer). 'The lists' are the enclosed, roped-off fighting area prepared for a formal duel — the term comes from the wooden palisades ('listes') bounding a tournament field. God was supposed to grant victory to the innocent party.
detail: Trial by combat was the medieval legal mechanism for resolving an accusation when no other proof was available — the rationale being that divine providence would protect the innocent fighter. For commoners, the weapons were typically clubs or staffs with a sand-bag attached; the stage direction confirms this here. The armourer-apprentice duel is drawn from Holinshed, who records that in 1446 a servant accused his master of saying 'the Duke of York was rightful heir to the crown' and the two were made to fight. In Holinshed the master was drunk and was slain; Shakespeare retains this detail as a sign of God's verdict on the treason charge.

The roles of appellant and defendant in judicial combat, the derivation of 'lists' from the enclosed field, the sand-bag weapons (confirmed by the stage direction), and the Holinshed source for the 1446 armourer-apprentice duel are all accurate.

anchor_text: by his death we do perceive his guilt; And God in justice hath reveal'd to us The truth
summary: Henry is applying the theological logic of trial by combat: the loser dies because God has revealed his guilt. Horner's death — and especially his deathbed confession of treason — is taken as divine verdict that his accusation of York was true and that his apprentice Peter was in the right. This is the formal religious premise that made judicial combat a recognized legal procedure in medieval England.

Horner's dying confession ('I confess, I confess treason') clinches the matter, because it aligns his own words with the divine verdict the combat has just pronounced. The scene is simultaneously a comedy of a drunk man beaten by his terrified apprentice and a serious staging of God's justice — the play's pious king reads the latter with total sincerity, while the audience may note the irony that providence has expressed itself through sack and charneco.

anchor_text: we'll take her from the sheriff
summary: Eleanor enters 'in a white sheet' with a burning taper — the standard costume of public penance in medieval and Tudor England. A convicted penitent walked barefoot through public streets in an undyed or white garment, carrying a lit candle as a symbol of contrition, to be seen and mocked by the crowd. The earlier stage direction specifies this ritual costume and circumstance; the sheriff supervised the procession. Eleanor did this public penance historically in 1441.

'Papers on my back' (TLN 1099) refers to a written bill listing the offences, attached to the penitent's clothing so bystanders could read her crimes. Holinshed records that Eleanor Cobham 'was condemned to do open penance in three several places in London,' walking barefoot through the streets, and was then imprisoned for life. Shakespeare dramatizes the procession with close fidelity to his source.

anchor_text: dark shall be my light and night my day; To think upon my pomp shall be my hell
summary: Eleanor states her sentence of inner exile in two sharp antitheses — dark/light and night/day — and then names her punishment: to remember her former 'pomp' (splendor, public power) as torture. This is the de casibus pattern: the fall from glory is not only material but psychological, and the memory of greatness becomes its own hell.

Eleanor's formulation condenses the argument of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy II: the goods of Fortune cause more anguish when lost than if they had never been possessed. The same pattern drives her husband's impending tragedy.

The antithesis and de casibus framing are sound, but the detail claim that Eleanor 'condenses the argument of Boethius's Consolation II' over-reads the lines — she is expressing immediate grief, not deploying Boethian philosophy, and the Boethian attribution is an unforced importation not required by the text.

anchor_text: lim'd bushes to betray thy wings, And, fly thou how thou canst, they'll tangle thee
summary: Eleanor uses the image of bird-liming to warn Gloucester: Suffolk, York, and Cardinal Beaufort have coated every branch with sticky lime to trap him. 'Bird-lime' was a thick, gluey substance smeared on branches to catch small birds by their feet. No matter how cleverly a bird flew, it could not avoid the lime-smeared twigs set all around it — so Gloucester cannot escape the conspiracy laid against him by dodging individual moves.

The image works on two levels: literal (the hunters have covered every approach) and ironic (Eleanor, herself just caught, is warning the man who let it happen). The trap-imagery also anticipates Gloucester's arrest: he is 'wing'd' (raised up as Protector) but surrounded on every side.

anchor_text: I must offend before I be attainted
summary: 'Attainted' is the legal term for being formally convicted of a felony or treason, with the result that all property and civil rights are forfeited and 'blood is corrupted' — meaning the conviction also disqualifies one's heirs. Gloucester insists he cannot be legally destroyed unless he actually commits a crime first; his integrity is his only shield.
detail: An 'act of attainder' could be passed by Parliament without a normal trial, which is exactly how Gloucester's enemies will eventually move against him. His confidence here — 'I must offend before I be attainted' — is tragically naive about what his opponents are prepared to do: they will arrest him, and he will never be tried. The legal point is central to the play's political argument about the corruption of justice under a weak king.

anchor_text: he that loos'd them forth their brazen caves
summary: Margaret addresses Aeolus, the god of winds, who according to Greek myth kept the winds imprisoned in caves or a bag until releasing them at the command of the gods. Here Margaret curses Aeolus for letting the winds blow her toward England when they should have blown her back. 'Brazen' means made of brass; the caves are the god's bronze-forged prison for the storm-winds.
detail: In Virgil's Aeneid (1.50-86) Juno orders Aeolus to release the winds from their cave to scatter Aeneas's fleet; Homer's Odyssey (10.1-75) describes Aeolus giving Odysseus a bag containing the adverse winds. The 'brazen' (bronze) quality of the mythological cave is a conventional attribute. Shakespeare uses the Aeolus image in several plays; here it allows Margaret to cast herself as a Virgilian epic heroine buffeted by divine forces — a grandiose self-dramatization appropriate to her character.

anchor_text: Aeolus would not be a murtherer, But left that hateful office unto thee
summary: Margaret inverts the standard mythology: normally Aeolus releasing his storms drowns sailors — but here he refused to drown her, leaving the task (figuratively) to Henry, who would kill her with sorrow on land. This hyperbolic inversion — the winds are kind, the husband brutal — is characteristic of a persuasion speech designed to shame Henry into attending to Margaret rather than mourning Gloucester. Margaret is effectively competing with the dead man for Henry's grief.

summary: Warwick uses an extended simile comparing the angry commons to a leaderless beehive scattering in all directions. The image sets up the political threat Suffolk faces from below — the people, not just the nobles, want him dead.

summary: Warwick describes the normal appearance of a naturally dead corpse: 'timely-parted' means someone who died in the ordinary course of time, not by violence. anchor_text: his face is black and full of blood, His eyeballs further out than when he liv'd, Staring full ghastly like a strangled man
summary: Warwick describes what the corpse actually looks like: a face darkened by congested blood, bulging eyes, and signs of violent struggle — hair pulled loose, nostrils flared, hands spread as if grasping for life. The scene functions as an informal coroner's inquest: Warwick as witness-examiner, the body as evidence, and Suffolk as the implicit accused who must supply an innocent explanation. Shakespeare, following Holinshed, makes the case circumstantially damning even if no direct confession is given until the end of the play.

anchor_text: Who finds the heifer dead and bleeding fresh And sees fast by a butcher with an axe But will suspect 't was he that made the slaughter

anchor_text: Blunt-witted lord, ignoble in demeanour! If ever lady wrong'd her lord so much, Thy mother took into her blameful bed Some stern untutor'd churl

anchor_text: What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted! Thrice is he arm'd that hath his quarrel just
summary: Henry delivers a sententious couplet — a moral maxim or 'sentence': a clear conscience is better armor than any breastplate; a man fighting in a just cause is three times as well-armed as one in steel with a guilty cause. The idea was proverbial in the period and draws on both classical Stoic thought and Christian teaching about the 'breastplate of righteousness' (from St Paul's armor of God).
