It also echoes the Stoic commonplace (cf. Cicero, De Officiis 3.6) that only just action is truly strong. Henry's philosophical aside is characteristic: he is the play's most eloquent moralizer but its most politically helpless figure — the king who speaks better than he acts.

anchor_text: Bring me unto my trial when you will
summary: Beaufort's delirious outburst — 'trial,' 'Did he not in his bed? where should he die?' — is a guilty conscience speaking. The 'he' he fixates on is Gloucester, whose strangling the Cardinal helped arrange in the previous scene (3.2). Beaufort cannot die cleanly because he cannot stop reliving the murder.
detail: Shakespeare follows the chronicle tradition, drawn from Holinshed and Hall, that Cardinal Beaufort died in a state of despairing agitation that contemporaries read as divine punishment for Gloucester's death. Holinshed describes Beaufort as raving 'in such sort that it was woonder to heare' and offers the death as proof of guilt. The dramatic technique — accusation through broken, half-intelligible fragments ('Alive again? then show me where he is') — keeps the murder offstage while making its weight felt through the murderer's collapse. Warwick had already exposed the signs of strangling on Gloucester's corpse in 3.2; now the audience sees Beaufort's mind do the same work from the inside.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the death of Cardinal Beaufort (Henry Beaufort, Bishop of Winchester), 1447, following the death of the Duke of Gloucester.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1987

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record Beaufort's agitated death in the Henry VI section, and the claim that Shakespeare drew on this chronicle tradition for the raving deathbed scene is well established in Shakespeare scholarship; the citation to Holinshed 1587 on Beaufort's death in 1447 is real and supportive.

The fragmented guilty-conscience reading is fully grounded in the text's broken syntax and explicit references to trial and a dead man's body; Holinshed's account of Beaufort's agitated death as divine punishment for Gloucester is the standard source and the dramatic technique is mainstream.

anchor_text: Like lime-twigs set to catch my winged soul
summary: A lime-twig was a branch smeared with sticky birdlime (a gluey substance made from holly bark) and set as a trap to catch birds by their feet. Beaufort, hallucinating, sees the hairs standing on a dead man's head as a line of these traps waiting to snare his departing soul — which he imagines as a bird trying to flee his dying body.
detail: The image of the soul as a bird escaping the body at death was common in Elizabethan religious verse and emblem-books; limning the devil or death as a fowler setting snares for souls is a related topos (compare Psalm 91:3, Geneva 1599: 'He will deliver thee from the snare of the hunter'). Here the trap is constructed from hallucinated physical detail — the standing hair of what Beaufort imagines is Gloucester's body — which collapses the supernatural (a fiend hunting his soul) into the material (birdcatcher's gear). Birdlime was made by boiling down holly-bark or mistletoe berries; the process was described in standard husbandry manuals including Conrad Heresbach, Four Books of Husbandry (Englished 1577).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'lime-twig' n.: 'a twig smeared with birdlime, used as a snare for birds'; also s.v. 'birdlime' n. Compare the soul-as-bird trope in emblem literature, e.g. Geoffrey Whitney, A Choice of Emblemes (1586).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1995

OED s.v. 'lime-twig' is a genuine entry, Psalm 91:3 in Geneva 1599 reads 'He will deliuer thee from the snare of the hunter' (confirmed), Geoffrey Whitney's A Choice of Emblemes (1586) is a real text, and Conrad Heresbach's Four Books of Husbandry (Englished 1577) is a real husbandry manual; all cited sources exist and are consistent with the claims made.

The lime-twig-as-birdsnare gloss is accurate, the soul-as-bird-fleeing-the-body topos is well-attested in Elizabethan emblem and devotional literature, and the collapse of supernatural threat into hallucinated physical detail maps cleanly onto Beaufort's fractured speech.

anchor_text: beat away the busy meddling fiend
summary: Henry prays that God will drive away a devil actively besieging Beaufort's soul at the moment of death. Late-medieval and Elizabethan theology held that Satan and his demons fought hardest for a soul at the very instant of dying — the soul's last chance to despair and be damned, or to repent and be saved.
detail: The deathbed struggle between angels and demons for the departing soul was the subject of the enormously popular Ars Moriendi tradition (Latin: 'the art of dying'), a genre of guides to a good death that circulated across Europe from the fifteenth century in print. The Ars Moriendi manuals described five temptations a dying person faced — loss of faith, despair, impatience, spiritual pride, and avarice — each driven by specific demons, each answered by a guardian angel. An 'evil death,' with the dying person raving, despairing, or unrepentant, was read as demonic victory. Beaufort's behavior — delirious, guilt-ridden, unable to make any sign of hope when asked — fits the template of a soul that the fiend has won. Warwick's verdict in the next line ('So bad a death argues a monstrous life') repeats the Ars Moriendi logic exactly.

sources.name: Ars Moriendi tradition
sources.citation: Ars Moriendi (c. 1415), widely printed in England; William Caxton printed an English version c. 1491. The five deathbed temptations are surveyed in Mary Catharine O'Connor, The Art of Dying Well (1942), ch. 1-2.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2000

The Ars Moriendi (c. 1415) is a real genre with exactly the five temptations listed (lack of faith, despair, impatience, spiritual pride, avarice); Caxton's English version is real though the date is 1490 not c. 1491 (a minor variant found in some secondary sources); O'Connor's The Art of Dying Well (1942, Columbia University Press) is a confirmed scholarly publication; all sources support the claims.

The Ars Moriendi framework for the deathbed struggle between angel and demon is mainstream for Elizabethan theology, and Beaufort's inability to respond to Henry's hopeful prompt (TLN 2007-2008) enacts precisely the demonic-victory template the annotation describes.

anchor_text: So bad a death argues a monstrous life
summary: Warwick concludes that a wretched death proves a wretched life. Henry counters with what was recognized as scripture: 'Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all' restates Jesus's warning in Matthew 7:1, 'Judge not, that ye be not judged' (Geneva 1599). The exchange sets two Elizabethan instincts against each other: the Ars Moriendi expectation that how you die reveals your soul's state, and the Christian prohibition on judging another's salvation.
detail: Henry's rebuke is not merely pious softness; in the dramatic context it is also a quiet mark of his character — he is too gentle for the political world around him, and his refusal to condemn even a man who helped murder his uncle is both theologically correct and politically disabling. The tension between Warwick's hard verdict and Henry's mercy is structural in the play: it is because Henry will not act that men like Beaufort, Suffolk, and eventually York can act against him without fear of royal retribution. Romans 2:1 (Geneva 1599) reinforces the point: 'Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest another.'

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 7:1 (Geneva 1599): 'Iudge not, that ye be not iudged.' Compare Romans 2:1 (Geneva 1599).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2009

Matthew 7:1 in Geneva 1599 is confirmed as 'Iudge not, that ye be not iudged'; Romans 2:1 in Geneva 1599 is confirmed as 'Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoeuer thou art that condemnest' — the annotation paraphrases it with 'judgest' rather than quoting directly, but the verse is real and relevant; both citations genuinely support the gloss.

Matthew 7:1 is a natural and well-attested source for 'Forbear to judge,' and the reading of Henry's mercy as simultaneously theologically correct and politically disabling is a defensible and mainstream character interpretation for this play.

anchor_text: gaudy, blabbing, and remorseful day
summary: The Captain opens with a sustained personification of day as a gossiping, guilt-ridden informer who has crept away, allowing the wolves of night to drag their horses across the sky and breathe plague into the air. 'Blabbing' casts daylight as something that would expose the murder about to happen; 'remorseful' means full of pity or regret. The speech frames Suffolk's execution as an act of night justice.
detail: The night-horses ('jades') and 'flagging wings' personify night as a slow, decayed creature rather than a chariot — the opposite of Homer's rosy-fingered dawn. 'Clip' means 'embrace'; 'jaws' continues the devouring imagery. The passage belongs to the Elizabethan topos of night as the accomplice of violent deeds, familiar from Macbeth's 'Come, seeling night' and Richard III's dark openings.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blabbing' (disclosing secrets); s.v. 'remorseful' (compassionate, regretful); s.v. 'clip' v.1 (to embrace or encircle).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2013
OED entries for 'blabbing' (disclosing secrets), 'remorseful' (compassionate/regretful), and 'clip' v.1 (to embrace) are real and accurately support the archaic meanings claimed.

The personification of day as informer/witness and night as a decayed, plague-breathing creature is firmly grounded in the text's own imagery (jades, flagging wings, jaws, contagious darkness) and the Elizabethan night-as-accomplice topos is mainstream-defensible.

anchor_text: our pinnace anchors in the Downs
summary: A 'pinnace' is a small, fast sailing vessel used as a tender or scout-ship for a larger fleet. 'The Downs' is a famous anchorage in the English Channel off the coast of Kent, sheltered by the Goodwin Sands — the same stretch of water through which ships travelling between England and France would pass. The Captain's crew has paused there long enough to execute the prisoners on the shore.
detail: The Downs (off Deal and Walmer in Kent) was the standard holding-ground for ships waiting for wind or awaiting orders. That Suffolk is captured in these waters near Kent is significant: Kent is also the county where Jack Cade's rebellion is simultaneously brewing (the Captain notes 'The commons here in Kent are up in arms'), suggesting a convergence of threats around the same geography.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pinnace' n. (a small sailing vessel, often used as a tender); OED s.v. 'Downs' (the famous anchorage off the coast of Kent, between the shore and the Goodwin Sands).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2021
OED s.v. 'pinnace' (small sailing vessel) and 'Downs' (the Kent anchorage off the Goodwin Sands) are real entries that accurately support the summary.

Both glosses are accurate: a pinnace is a small fast vessel and the Downs is the Kent anchorage; the geographic connection to the simultaneous Kentish rebellion is a defensible contextual observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: make boot of this
summary: 'Make boot' means to take profit or plunder from something — 'boot' here is booty or gain. The Captain is dividing up the captured prisoners as prizes of war: each captor gets to ransom (or kill) his assigned prisoner and pocket the proceeds.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'boot' n.2 (profit, gain, booty).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2025
Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'boot' n.2 (profit, gain, booty) is a real entry that directly supports the gloss.
'Make boot' meaning to take plunder or profit is straightforward Elizabethan usage and fits the Captain's action of distributing prisoners as prizes.

anchor_text: Look on my George; I am a gentleman
summary: A 'George' is the jewelled badge of the Order of the Garter, England's highest order of knighthood, showing Saint George slaying the dragon. Suffolk is pointing to it as proof of his rank — a knight of the Garter is by definition a great nobleman, whose life should be worth ransom rather than summary execution. The gesture is an appeal to social hierarchy that the Captain will brutally dismiss.
detail: The Order of the Garter was founded by Edward III around 1348 and limited to 24 knights plus the sovereign; membership was the mark of the highest chivalric distinction. The 'George' (the badge itself, also called the 'Lesser George' when worn on a ribbon) would have been immediately legible to an Elizabethan audience as a symbol of supreme social status. Suffolk's appeal to it underlines both his arrogance and the scene's central irony: his rank cannot save him.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Order of the Garter and the 'George' badge; cf. Elias Ashmole, The Institution, Laws and Ceremonies of the Most Noble Order of the Garter (1672), on the 'George' as the order's pendant badge.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2041
The Order of the Garter's foundation by Edward III c.1348 with 24 knights is historically accurate; Ashmole's 1672 monograph on the Garter is a real work that documents the 'George' pendant badge.
The 'George' as the Garter badge is historically accurate; Suffolk's gesture as an appeal to rank that is brushed aside is clearly what the text dramatises, and the irony reading is well-supported.

anchor_text: Thy name affrights me, in whose sound is death
summary: The name 'Walter' was commonly pronounced 'Water' in Elizabethan English, so the prophesied death 'by water' is literally contained in the name of Suffolk's killer. Suffolk tries to escape the pun by insisting Whitmore's name is really 'Gaultier' (the French or Norman form of the same name), but Whitmore refuses the rebranding. The pun makes Whitmore's identity itself the fulfilment of fate.
detail: The joke is a grim play on phonetics: Elizabethan spelling and pronunciation frequently rendered 'Wa-' as 'Wa-ter' (the OED records the 'Water' pronunciation of 'Walter' as standard). Shakespeare's audience would catch the pun instantly. 'Gaultier' is the French cognate of the Germanic 'Walter' — Suffolk's attempt to invoke the French form both shows his aristocratic preference for French and is a futile dodge. Holinshed records the water-prophecy and Whitmore's role.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Walter' (the name, with note on the common Elizabethan pronunciation rhyming with 'water'); Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'Gaultier' (the French/Norman form of 'Walter').

The Walter/water pun is editorially well-attested, but the OED does not have a standalone entry for the proper name 'Walter' documenting the Elizabethan 'water' pronunciation as a lexical citation; the source as stated cannot be verified exactly.

The Walter/water homophony is a documented Elizabethan pronunciation and the text makes the pun explicit: Suffolk immediately tries to escape it by insisting on 'Gaultier,' confirming the audience is meant to hear 'water' in 'Walter.'

anchor_text: A cunning man did calculate my birth
summary: A 'cunning man' is a practitioner of astrology or folk magic who reads the stars at a person's birth to foretell their fate — here, that Suffolk would die by water. This prophecy was delivered in 1.4 of the play, when Eleanor Cobham's conjured spirit listed the fates of the great lords; 'Suffolk shall die by water' was one of its riddles. The name 'Walter' contains 'water,' making Whitmore the instrument of the prophecy's fulfilment.
detail: Predicting a nobleman's death was treasonable in Tudor England; the conjuring scene (1.4) dramatizes the real 1441 trial of Eleanor Cobham and her accomplices, including Roger Bolingbroke. That Suffolk recognizes the prophecy's fulfilment the moment he hears the name 'Walter' shows the Elizabethan audience's familiarity with the idea of prophecies that are both exact and cruelly misleading — fulfilled in a sense the recipient never anticipated.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Eleanor Cobham's conjuring and the prophetic spirit's words; also Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2046
Holinshed (1587) and Hall (1548) are the standard chronicle sources for Eleanor Cobham's conjuring and the Suffolk water-prophecy; both are real and directly support the summary.

The back-reference to the 1.4 prophecy is explicit in Suffolk's own words ('by water I should die'), and the conjuring scene's historical basis in Eleanor Cobham's 1441 trial is well-documented in Holinshed.

anchor_text: Jove sometime went disguis'd, and why not I
summary: Jove (Jupiter, king of the gods) repeatedly disguised himself in classical myth to walk among mortals — as a bull, a swan, a mortal man — usually for amorous purposes. Suffolk claims that wearing a disguise is not beneath a great man. The Captain demolishes the parallel immediately: Jove was never killed in disguise, as Suffolk is about to be.
detail: The most common Ovidian instances are Jupiter's disguise as a bull to abduct Europa (Metamorphoses 2.836-875) and as a swan to approach Leda (Met. 6.109). Suffolk's analogy is self-flattering and imprecise; the Captain's riposte — 'But Jove was never slain, as thou shalt be' — cuts it off with blunt logic. The exchange also frames Suffolk's pride: even in rags he reaches for divine comparison and finds only a fatal one.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875 (Jupiter as bull, abducting Europa); 6.109 (Jupiter as swan); in Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2060

Suffolk's Jove-in-disguise conceit is supported by the text and the Captain's instant rebuttal ('But Jove was never slain') confirms the exchange works exactly as glossed; the Ovidian examples cited are standard and appropriate.

anchor_text: Bare-headed plodded by my foot-cloth mule
summary: A 'foot-cloth' was a large, richly ornamented cloth draped over a horse or mule and hanging almost to the ground — a display of status reserved for the very great, because it demonstrated the owner could afford a slow, ceremonial pace. Walking 'bare-headed' beside a superior's mounted animal was an act of enforced humility and service. Suffolk taunts Whitmore by reminding him that he once served in exactly this degrading role, walking hatless at Suffolk's stirrup.
detail: The foot-cloth was a recognized indicator of rank; sumptuary thinking governed how elaborate a noble's horse-trappings could be. Suffolk's litany of Whitmore's past service — holding the stirrup, plodding bare-headed, waiting at the cup, kneeling at the board — is designed to reduce the sailor to a household menial who has stepped catastrophically above his station. The rhetoric of degree and service runs through this speech and connects to the broader Great Chain of Being anxiety the history plays dramatize.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'foot-cloth' n. (an ornamental cloth hung over a horse's back to the ground, a mark of dignity); Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'foot-cloth.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2066
OED s.v. 'foot-cloth' (ornamental cloth hung to the ground from a horse, a mark of dignity) and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary entry are real and accurately support the cultural gloss.

The foot-cloth as a mark of dignity and walking bare-headed as enforced humility are accurately glossed; Suffolk's catalogue of Whitmore's past services is plainly in the text (TLN 2065-2074) and the social-hierarchy reading is sound.

anchor_text: Pool! Sir Pool! lord!
summary: The Captain plays on the multiple meanings of Suffolk's family name 'de la Pole': 'Pole' sounds like 'pool' (a stagnant, dirty body of water), and he immediately riffs through 'kennel' (a street gutter), 'puddle,' and 'sink' (a cesspool) — all images of filth and polluted water choking England's clean spring. The pun reduces the Duke's aristocratic French surname to sewage, accusing him of corrupting the realm.
detail: The de la Pole family was one of the great English noble houses; their name, of French origin, had no vulgar English connotation — which is exactly why the Captain's forced rhyme with 'pool/puddle/sink' is an act of verbal violence. The water imagery that closes the speech ironically rhymes with the water-prophecy about Suffolk's death: he who has corrupted England's spring will die in the sea. The speech is also a conscious inversion of the heraldic language Suffolk used when he cited his George badge — the Captain answers aristocratic dignity with street-gutter vocabulary.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'kennel' n.2 (the channel or gutter of a street); s.v. 'sink' n. (a drain, a cesspool).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2085
Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'kennel' n.2 (street gutter) and 'sink' n. (drain, cesspool) are real entries that support the wordplay annotation.
The Pole/pool pun is explicit in the Captain's own escalation through 'kennel, puddle, sink' and the de la Pole family name makes the verbal violence precise; the gloss does not overreach.

anchor_text: thou that smil'dst at good Duke Humphrey's death
summary: The Captain accuses Suffolk of having connived at the murder of Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester — 'good Duke Humphrey,' the Lord Protector — who was strangled in his bed at Bury St Edmunds in Act 3. Suffolk was the architect of Gloucester's arrest and the man who arranged the killing; the commons' loss of their protector is the political catastrophe that makes Suffolk's own death feel, to the Captain, like rough justice.
detail: Gloucester's murder (3.2) was Shakespeare's dramatization of the historical death of Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1447. Warwick exposed the murder from the marks on the corpse; the commons demanded Suffolk's punishment. Here the pirate-Captain voices the popular anger that drove Suffolk's banishment — the same anger that drove the ship onto the seas where he now dies.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Humphrey Duke of Gloucester's death at Bury St Edmunds, 1447, and Suffolk's implication in it.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2091
Holinshed (1587) records Humphrey Duke of Gloucester's death at Bury St Edmunds in 1447 and Suffolk's implication; the citation accurately supports the historical claim.
The accusation that Suffolk connived at Gloucester's murder is the play's own established plot (3.2) and the popular anger driving Suffolk's banishment and death is accurately presented.

anchor_text: like ambitious Sylla, overgorg'd
summary: Sulla (spelled 'Sylla' in Elizabethan texts) was the Roman general and dictator who, in 82-79 BCE, seized Rome by force and carried out mass executions called proscriptions — posting lists of enemies to be killed and confiscating their estates. The Captain compares Suffolk to Sulla to name him a man who fattened himself on his own country's blood: 'gobbets of thy mother's bleeding heart' means chunks of England's bleeding flesh.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Sulla (in North's 1579 translation) was Shakespeare's likely source; Sulla was the standard classical example of a powerful man who used proscription — the state-sanctioned murder of political rivals — to enrich himself and destroy opposition. The comparison is precise: Suffolk, the Captain charges, has acted like a Roman dictator inside England itself, devouring the body politic from within rather than defending it from foreign foes.

sources.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Sulla (Sylla), in Thomas North's translation, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579), on Sulla's proscriptions of 82-79 BCE.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2099
Plutarch's Life of Sulla in North's 1579 translation is a real source; Sulla's proscriptions of 82-79 BCE and his seizure of power through mass executions are accurately described.

Sulla/Sylla as the type of a proscription-wielding self-enriching tyrant is the standard classical comparison and the metaphor of 'gobbets of thy mother's bleeding heart' making him 'overgorg'd' fits the Sullan proscription parallel precisely.

anchor_text: half-fac'd sun, striving to shine, Under the which is writ 'Invitis nubibus.'
summary: The 'half-faced sun' is the heraldic badge of the House of York — a sun emerging from behind clouds, which was adopted by Edward IV (York's son) and used by the Yorkist cause. The Latin motto 'Invitis nubibus' means 'In spite of the clouds' or 'Despite the clouds that oppose' — expressing the Yorkist claim that their sun-right to the crown cannot be permanently obscured. The Captain is saying that York's rising power is already visible and cannot be stopped.
detail: The sunburst emblem had deep personal meaning for the Yorkists: Edward IV was said to have seen three suns in the sky at the battle of Mortimer's Cross (1461) and taken it as a divine omen. In Richard III (5.3) the same imagery appears when Richard wakes to a sun obscured. 'Half-faced' here means the sun is only half-visible, still partly behind clouds — a statement of the Yorkist claim not yet fully realized. The motto reinforces the heraldic image with explicit defiance: the clouds (the Lancastrian opposition) cannot permanently blot out the sun.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Yorkist sun badge and the house of York's claim to the crown; cf. Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2113
Holinshed (1587) and Hall (1548) are the real chronicle sources for the Yorkist sun badge and its dynastic symbolism; the three-suns omen at Mortimer's Cross is recorded by Holinshed.

The sun badge is a Yorkist emblem and 'Invitis nubibus' is a plausible gloss, but the specific claim that it was Edward IV's personal badge adopted after the three-suns omen at Mortimer's Cross (1461) is anachronistic here — the play is set c. 1450, a decade before that battle — and the exact motto's attribution requires verification; the core heraldic reading is defensible but the Edward IV detail is an overreach.

anchor_text: Murther'd sweet Tully; Brutus' bastard hand / Stabb'd Julius Caesar; savage islanders / Pompey the Great
summary: Suffolk's dying speech lists three great Romans killed by low or treacherous hands: Cicero ('Tully,' his family name Tullius) murdered by hired soldiers on Antony's orders in 43 BCE; Julius Caesar stabbed by Brutus — called 'bastard' because one tradition held Brutus was Caesar's illegitimate son; and Pompey the Great, murdered by an Egyptian soldier after fleeing the battle of Pharsalus (48 BCE). Suffolk places himself alongside these victims to insist that great men have always been brought low by vile agents.
detail: The three examples are drawn from Plutarch's Lives (North 1579). Cicero's death at the hands of Antony's agents is in Plutarch's Life of Cicero and Life of Antony; Caesar's murder by Brutus in the Life of Caesar and Life of Brutus; Pompey's murder by Egyptian soldiers in the Life of Pompey. 'Bastard' as applied to Brutus reflects the ancient rumor (reported by Plutarch, Life of Caesar 62) that Caesar had an affair with Brutus's mother Servilia, making Brutus potentially Caesar's son — the added horror that a son stabbed his father. 'Savage islanders' refers to the Egyptians who killed Pompey on the Egyptian shore, called 'savage' to heighten the indignity of dying at non-Roman hands — as Suffolk is dying at the hands of pirates.

sources.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Pompey 77-79 (Pompey murdered in Egypt, 48 BCE); Life of Caesar 62 (the Brutus-as-bastard-son rumor); Life of Cicero 47-48 (Cicero killed on Antony's orders, 43 BCE); in Thomas North's translation (1579).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2151

Plutarch Life of Pompey 77-79 (murder in Egypt), Life of Caesar 62 (Brutus-as-bastard-son rumor via Servilia), and Life of Cicero 47-48 (Cicero killed on Antony's orders, 43 BCE) are all real chapters with content that directly supports the three examples cited.

All three classical examples are accurately identified and sourced to Plutarch; the 'bastard hand' gloss correctly explains the ancient tradition that Brutus was Caesar's son by Servilia, and 'savage islanders' for the Egyptians who killed Pompey fits the text and the parallel Suffolk draws between himself and great men killed by vile agents.

anchor_text: get thee a sword, though made of a lath
summary: A lath is a thin strip of wood. Bevis is joking that any weapon will do for a peasant army. Swords made of lath were the prop-weapons of stage clowns and comic Vice figures in popular morality plays, so the line simultaneously mocks the ragtag rebellion — real soldiers carry steel.
detail: The Vice of Tudor morality drama routinely carried a wooden sword or dagger of lath as his comic weapon. Bevis's joke thus codes the rebellion as a piece of low theatre even before Cade appears — the rebels know their uprising is a kind of performance.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'lath, n.2': 'a thin flat strip of wood'; and s.v. 'dagger of lath': the Vice's comic weapon.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2163
OED s.v. 'lath, n.2' and s.v. 'dagger of lath' are real entries supporting both the material definition and the Vice's comic-weapon convention.
The Vice's dagger/sword of lath is a well-documented stage convention; the reading that Bevis codes the rebellion as low theatre is a mainstream defensible inference from the context.

anchor_text: Jack Cade the clothier means to dress the commonwealth, and turn it, and set a new nap upon it
summary: Bevis packs in three cloth-trade puns. 'Dress' means both 'reform' and 'prepare cloth for use.' 'Turn' means both 'change' and 'turn the nap' — the fuzzy surface of woolen fabric — to refresh a worn garment. 'Set a new nap' means restore a fresh surface, as a clothier would revive threadbare wool. The joke is that Cade promises a total makeover of England using the vocabulary of his trade.

summary: Holland twists the Protestant doctrine that every Christian should serve God faithfully in their own 'calling' or 'vocation' — a central Reformation idea drawn from 1 Corinthians 7:20 ('Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called'). anchor_text: We John Cade, so term'd of our supposed father
summary: Cade opens with mock-royal 'We' — the formal plural used by monarchs — and then claims to be named 'Cade' only after his supposed father, hinting his real surname is Mortimer. The Mortimers were the family through whom the Duke of York traced his claim to the throne (via the female line of Edward III's second surviving son). By pretending to be a Mortimer, Cade is providing York with a disposable pretender: if the revolt succeeds, York benefits; if it fails, Cade takes the blame.

anchor_text: My mother a Plantagenet
summary: Plantagenet was the royal dynasty that had ruled England from Henry II (1154) through Richard III (1485). Cade claims royal blood through his mother, which Dick immediately deflates: she was a midwife. 'The Lacies' (TLN 2198), the family Cade claims for his wife, were a real Anglo-Norman noble house, and 'laces' (TLN 2200) is a pun on the name: she merely sold ribbons at market.
detail: The Plantagenet name was not actually used by the medieval kings themselves as a family surname; it was retrospectively applied. anchor_text: his coat is of proof
summary: 'Proof' in armor means tested and hardened against sword-blows — 'proof-armor' could not be cut. anchor_text: seven halfpenny loaves sold for a penny; the three-hooped pot shall have ten hoops; and I will make it felony to drink small beer. All the realm shall be in common
summary: Cade's promises are a comic utopian manifesto targeting real grievances. Bread prices and ale-measure were regulated by the Assize of Bread and Ale — a medieval statute enforcing standard loaf sizes and pot-measures. A 'three-hooped pot' was a standard tankard marked by three iron hoops to show approved measure; Cade promises to increase the hoops (and thus the drink). 'All the realm shall be in common' echoes the 1381 Peasants' Revolt demand for the abolition of private property.

anchor_text: The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers
summary: Dick the Butcher's line is 2 Henry VI's most-quoted sentence. In context it is not random violence: Cade immediately connects lawyers to parchment (legal documents), which could bind a man to a debt or tenancy for life. The rebels hate the written law because it is the mechanism by which landlords, creditors, and the crown control the illiterate poor. Cade adds that it is the beeswax seal on a legal document — not the sting — that has enslaved him: he 'sealed once to a thing' (signed a bond) and was never his own man again.

For the unlettered commoner, written contracts and court records were instruments of oppression wielded by the literate class on those who could not read what they were signing. The whole Clerk of Chartham sequence that follows stages the same fear of literacy as a tool of power.

anchor_text: Has a book in his pocket with red letters in 't
summary: Smith says the Clerk carries a book with red lettering — which in this period meant a printed almanac, a legal primer, or a service book, since red ink was used for headings, feast days, and rubrics in liturgical texts (hence 'red-letter day'). Cade immediately calls it proof of conjuring. For the rebels, any writing or printed book is a sign of dangerous, elite knowledge — the same logic that makes the Clerk's literacy a death sentence.

The confusion with conjuring (TLN 2242) is entirely coherent given that Roger Bolingbroke the conjurer was arrested earlier in the play (1.4) partly for possessing forbidden books.

anchor_text: hast thou a mark to thyself, like a honest, plain-dealing man
summary: An illiterate person who could not write their name used a 'mark' — a personal symbol such as a cross or a simple drawn device — as a legal signature. The joke inverts normal values: literacy becomes a vice, illiteracy a virtue.

In legal documents it appears as 'his mark' next to a drawn symbol. Cade's reversal — treating the mark as a sign of honesty and writing as suspicious — is a precise comic inversion: the rebels' entire ideology turns the social hierarchy upside down, making manual and oral culture superior to literate culture.

anchor_text: boys went to span-counter for French crowns
summary: Span-counter was a children's street game in which players pitched coins toward a wall, the winner being whoever landed a coin within a hand-span of another. 'French crowns' were gold coins. Cade is saying that under Henry V — who conquered France — French gold was so abundant in England that even boys played pitch-and-toss with it. The remark sets up his offer to Henry VI: Cade will tolerate him as king, but only as Cade's own protectorate.

anchor_text: then are we in order when we are most out of order
summary: Cade's closing paradox inverts the political doctrine of 'order' and 'degree' — the Elizabethan belief that stable society depended on every rank keeping its appointed place. He declares that rebellion, which is precisely the disorder the authorities fear, is the rebels' true order. The line is an antimetabole (a figure that repeats words in reversed positions to make an opposite point), turning the language of authority against itself.
detail: The Homily Against Disobedience (1571), read in every English parish church, equated civil disorder with cosmic chaos. Cade's aphorism is a knowing joke at that doctrine: the mob's 'order' is the disorder of the overthrown hierarchy. The figure also captures the inversion logic that runs through the whole scene — literacy is treachery, illiteracy is virtue, a bricklayer is a king, and the 'commonwealth' is a piece of threadbare cloth to be re-dressed.

anchor_text: Lent shall be as long again as it is, and thou shalt have a licence to kill for a hundred lacking one
summary: In Elizabethan England, butchers were forbidden by law to sell meat during Lent (the 40-day fast before Easter), so a doubled Lent would mean 80 days a year when Dick could not legally trade. Cade's 'reward' is a comic mock-royal patent: instead of granting Dick wealth or land, he grants him an exemption from the religious restriction on slaughter. 'A licence to kill for a hundred lacking one' means a grant to slaughter 99 animals — just short of a clean round number, a jokingly exact quasi-legal formula.
detail: Elizabethan statutes on Lenten fasting (the 'Cecil fast,' periodically renewed through the 1560s-1590s) were as much about boosting the fishing trade and saving cattle as about religion; violators faced fines. The joke turns on the incongruity between high royal patronage and a butcher's trade, and on Cade's delusion that he already commands sovereign power to grant exemptions from statute. The phrasing 'a hundred lacking one' mimics the precise language of royal patents and writs, parodying legal form.

anchor_text: monument of the victory will I bear
summary: The stage direction specifies that Cade puts on Sir Humphrey Stafford's brigandine — a coat of body armor made of small iron or steel plates riveted inside leather or heavy cloth. By wearing the dead commander's armor as a 'monument of the victory,' Cade enacts a ritual of conquest: stripping a fallen enemy's arms and wearing them was a recognized way of displaying triumph. It is also a grotesque parody of the heraldic custom by which a victor displayed captured coats of arms.

The act visually stages the rebels' reversal of degree: a Kentish rebel drapes himself in a knight's arms and prepares to march on London. Holinshed notes that Cade's men wore harness stripped from the slain at the outset of the revolt.

anchor_text: bodies shall be dragged at my horse heels till I do come to London
summary: Dragging a condemned person at a horse's tail through the streets was the prescribed first stage of the official punishment for treason in England — traitors were drawn (dragged) to the place of execution before being hanged and quartered. Cade appropriates this royal penal ritual, applying it to the bodies of the king's own officers, inverting the state's authority: those who came to enforce order are now treated as traitors.
detail: The full sentence for high treason was to be 'drawn, hanged, and quartered': the felon was tied to a hurdle and dragged by horse to the gallows, symbolically denied the dignity of walking. By ordering the Staffords' bodies dragged to London, Cade mimics the spectacle of royal justice while marching in open rebellion against it — a theatrical usurpation of sovereign punishment. The gesture also echoes classical and medieval precedents for dishonoring an enemy's corpse (cf. Achilles dragging Hector at Troy), though Cade's frame of reference is more likely the public executions familiar to Elizabethan Londoners.

anchor_text: the mayor's sword borne before us
summary: The City of London's Lord Mayor was attended in all formal processions by an official sword-bearer who carried an upright ceremonial sword — the city's symbol of delegated royal justice — before him. Having the mayor's sword 'borne before' him would signal that Cade commands the civic dignity of the mayor himself. It is the clearest statement in the scene of Cade's fantasy: he is not a rebel but a ruler who will be received in London with the full honors of a sovereign.
detail: The sword of state carried before the monarch, and the corresponding civic sword carried before mayors and lord mayors, were among the most recognizable symbols of legitimate delegated authority in Elizabethan England; Edward Hall and other chroniclers record the ceremonial entries of kings into London with sword-bearers as a standard mark of royal power received. Cade's demand to have this honor performed for him is continuous with his other royal postures in Act 4 — receiving petitions, granting patents, pronouncing sentences — and collapses the moment his men are offered a royal pardon and desert him (4.8). The detail is present in the chronicle sources.

anchor_text: grief softens the mind And makes it fearful and degenerate
summary: Margaret opens with a Stoic argument — grief weakens resolve and makes a warrior 'degenerate' (unworthy of their lineage) — only to demolish it immediately with her own weeping. The speech is a self-contradiction performed in public, exposing how completely Suffolk's severed head has undone her rhetorical self-control.

Margaret knows the argument, invokes it as a directive ('Think therefore on revenge and cease to weep'), and in the very next breath confesses she cannot follow her own advice ('But who can cease to weep and look on this?'). The collapse is the dramatic point: the queen who has been the dominant political operator throughout the play is here momentarily levelled by private grief. The word 'degenerate' carries the Elizabethan sense of 'fallen from one's ancestral worth' — a pointed charge from a woman whose royal blood she wears as her chief credential.

anchor_text: like a wandering planet, over me
summary: In Elizabethan astronomy, 'planets' were the seven celestial bodies — Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn — that appeared to 'wander' against the fixed background of the stars. Margaret is saying Suffolk's face held sway over her the way a planet governs those born under its sign: irresistibly, by nature.
detail: The word 'planet' comes from Greek planetes, 'wanderer,' because these bodies moved against the fixed stars. In the Ptolemaic model taught in grammar schools and pulpits, the seven planets circled the earth in concentric spheres, and each ruled a day of the week, a metal, a body part, and a temperament. To say a face 'ruled like a wandering planet' is not mere poetry — it invokes the deterministic force of celestial influence, presenting Margaret's infatuation as something inevitable, written in the heavens. The aside is also loaded with dramatic irony: the face that ruled her so completely is now severed from its body and sits in her arms.

anchor_text: Jack Cade proclaims himself Lord Mortimer, Descended from the Duke of Clarence' house
summary: Cade's claim to the name 'Lord Mortimer' is a serious dynastic challenge: the Mortimer family inherited the claim of Lionel, Duke of Clarence — Edward III's second surviving son — which by strict birth order actually outranked the Lancastrian line. By styling himself 'Mortimer,' Cade is parroting York's own genealogical argument.

His daughter Philippa married Edmund Mortimer, 3rd Earl of March, and the Mortimer claim passed through female descent to Roger Mortimer, 4th Earl of March, then to his son Edmund, 5th Earl — who died childless and whose heir was Richard, Duke of York. Because Clarence ranked above Lancaster (John of Gaunt, Edward's third son) in birth order, Yorkist genealogists argued their title was superior to the reigning Lancastrian kings. Holinshed records that the historical Cade called himself 'John Mortimer' (Chronicles, 1587); Shakespeare adds the dynastic freight by having the Messenger use it to report what the rebels call Henry a 'usurper openly.' The play thus uses Cade's populist uprising as a transparent stalking-horse for York's aristocratic ambition: the same word that will justify York's rebellion in the next act.

anchor_text: All scholars, lawyers, courtiers, gentlemen, They call false caterpillars
summary: 'Caterpillars' was a standard Elizabethan political insult for those who devour the commonwealth for private gain — parasites who strip the realm bare as caterpillars strip a plant. That Cade's rebels apply it to scholars, lawyers, and courtiers reflects the rebellion's anti-literate, anti-legal program: literacy and written law are the tools by which the propertied classes exploit the commons.

The insult recurs because it names a specific, resented type: the place-seeker or monopolist who profits from royal favor at the expense of the broader political community. For Cade's rebels the category expands to everyone who can read and write — the entire administrative class whose literacy underwrites the law records and property deeds that bind the commons. Dick the Butcher's 'kill all the lawyers' (4.2) is the same grievance in a punchline.

anchor_text: they know not what they do
summary: Henry's cry echoes Christ's words from the cross — 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do' (Luke 23:34) — said of the soldiers crucifying him. The parallel is not accidental: Henry throughout the play is framed as a Christ-like innocent, passive and forgiving, destroyed by forces he cannot control. The allusion quietly casts the rebels as unwitting agents of a greater wickedness and the King as a sacrificial victim.
detail: The Geneva Bible (1560 and 1599) renders Luke 23:34: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' Henry's line is not an explicit quotation but a deliberate echo that first audiences, who heard the Gospels read aloud in church every Sunday, would catch immediately. The king's instinct is mercy rather than anger ('so many simple souls / Should perish by the sword'); he resembles Christ in offering intercession for those who threaten him. The irony the scene sustains is structural: Henry's piety and passivity are exactly what makes him unable to save himself or his kingdom. His Christ-likeness is both genuinely admirable and politically fatal.

anchor_text: retire to Killingworth
summary: 'Killingworth' is the contemporary Elizabethan form of Kenilworth, a royal castle in Warwickshire about 100 miles northwest of London and a traditional royal refuge. The name comes from Old English 'Cynehilde's worth' (an enclosed settlement); by Shakespeare's day it was routinely spelled 'Killingworth' in chronicles and on stage. Buckingham is advising the King to get out of London and put armed distance between himself and Cade's rebels.
detail: Kenilworth Castle was an enormous fortified palace, one of the great royal strongholds of medieval England, substantially built and extended by John of Gaunt in the late fourteenth century and inherited by the Lancastrian kings. Its removal to the Midlands made it the obvious bolt-hole when London was threatened; the historical Henry VI did withdraw from London during the Cade crisis of 1450. The castle's other association for Shakespeare's audience was the spectacular entertainment staged there for Elizabeth I in 1575 by Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — described in Robert Laneham's letter, a text Shakespeare almost certainly knew. Holinshed consistently uses the spelling 'Killingworth.'

anchor_text: rebels have assay'd to win the Tower

anchor_text: get you to Smithfield and gather head
summary: 'Gather head' means to muster soldiers or assemble a fighting force — 'head' here is short for 'a head of men,' a body of troops raised for action. Smithfield was an open ground just outside the city walls, northwest of the Tower and long used for musters, executions, and fairs, making it a natural rallying point. Scales is directing the citizens to meet the force he is about to send them.

Its selection here is practical: it lies between the Tower and the direction from which Cade's forces were pressing. The phrase 'gather head' appears elsewhere in Shakespeare's histories in this military sense (cf. 3 Henry VI 1.1: 'if we gather head'). Scales's instruction is thus both a rallying order and a map of the topography of the battle for London.

anchor_text: Now is Mortimer lord of this city
summary: Cade enters London calling himself 'Mortimer,' the dynastic alias York has coached him to use. anchor_text: set London bridge on fire; and, if you can, burn down the Tower too
summary: London Bridge was the only bridge over the Thames in the city, and whoever controlled it controlled movement between London and the south — including supply lines and any army coming from Kent. The Tower of London was the royal fortress, armory, and prison; holding it meant holding the crown's weapons, its treasury, and the ability to imprison enemies. Cade's orders target the two most strategic points in the city: cut the bridge, neutralize the royal stronghold.

Shakespeare compresses the events and places the bridge-burning order before the Smithfield battle, but the strategic logic is exact — destroying the bridge would trap rebel forces in the city and deny the King a route back in, while taking the Tower would give the rebels the crown's own guns and a power-base to hold London indefinitely. That Cade adds 'if you can' for the Tower reflects that it was successfully defended (the play has already shown Lord Scales in command of it, 4.5).

anchor_text: pull down the Savoy; others to the inns of court
summary: The Savoy was a palace on the Thames belonging to John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster; it was burned to the ground by Wat Tyler's rebels in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Cade's first orders echo that uprising almost exactly. The Inns of Court were the four law schools (Lincoln's Inn, Gray's Inn, the Inner and Middle Temple) where England's lawyers trained; burning them meant abolishing the legal profession.

By invoking the Savoy, Shakespeare signals the maximum limit of rebellion as his audience imagined it.

anchor_text: burn all the records of the realm. My mouth shall be the parliament
summary: Cade declares he will destroy all written law and govern by spoken decree alone. 'Records' means the written statutes and court rolls that define property rights, debts, and legal obligations. anchor_text: thou say, thou serge, nay, thou buckram lord
summary: Cade mocks Lord Say by running through a ladder of fabrics in descending quality: 'say' (a fine wool), 'serge' (a coarser weave), 'buckram' (cheap stiffened cloth used for lining). anchor_text: he has a familiar under his tongue; he speaks not o' God's name
summary: A 'familiar' (or familiar spirit) was a demon believed to serve a witch or sorcerer, often thought to reside inside the witch's body. Cade accuses Say of being a sorcerer — his eloquent speech is not natural human persuasion but a devil speaking through him. This explains why, just after confessing 'I feel remorse,' Cade reverses himself: Say's convincing words must be supernatural trickery, not honest argument.
detail: The accusation echoes the play's earlier witchcraft subplot (Eleanor Cobham, Margery Jourdain, and Roger Bolingbroke, 1.4), giving the Cade scenes a thematic link to the larger concern with magic and illegitimate power. The belief that witches housed familiar spirits within their bodies — in a teat, a finger, or under the tongue — was current in Elizabethan demonology and appears in the 1604 Witchcraft Act's list of offenses. By invoking the familiar, Cade avoids having to engage with Say's argument.

sources.name: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584)
sources.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), Book 3, on familiar spirits and their habitation within witches' bodies.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2534

Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) is a real source that covers familiar spirits, but the claim that Book 3 specifically treats 'habitation within witches' bodies' cannot be confirmed — the Book 3 table of contents is not accessible for direct verification and Scot's coverage of familiars spans multiple books.

The accusation of a familiar spirit under the tongue as Elizabethan demonological belief is well-documented; the thematic link to the Eleanor Cobham witchcraft subplot is a genuine structural parallel in the play and not an overreach.

anchor_text: maid be married but she shall pay to me her maidenhead ere they have it. Men shall hold of me in capite
summary: Cade announces a mock-feudal code: maidens must 'pay' him their virginity ('maidenhead') before they marry. This parodies the medieval custom of 'droit du seigneur' — a supposed lord's right to the first night with a new bride. 'Hold of me in capite' is a real legal phrase (Latin: 'by the head') for the most direct form of feudal land tenure, holding directly from the king — but Cade's 'capite' also puns on 'caput' (head), linking the feudal tribute to the beheadings he has just ordered.
detail: The 'droit du seigneur' (also called 'jus primae noctis') was more a legal fiction and satirical target than a universally practiced custom, but it circulated as an emblem of tyrannical lordship. Cade's claim fits the scene's pattern of grotesque parody: he parodies a parliament, parodies a trial, and now parodies a lord distributing land-law. 'Holding in capite' was the tenure by which lands were held directly of the king rather than through an intermediate lord — technically the grandest form of tenure. The double meaning (head/beheading + legal capite) is characteristic of the scene's dark comedy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'capite' (in fee simple, held directly of the Crown; from Latin caput, head).

sources.name: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law (1895)
sources.citation: Pollock, F. and Maitland, F. W., The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, 2nd ed. (1898), Vol. 1, pp. 232-235, on tenure in capite.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2547

OED s.v. 'capite' is a real entry defining tenure held directly of the Crown; Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law (2nd ed. 1898) vol. 1 is a real work that covers tenure in capite in its treatment of feudal land tenure.

The 'holding in capite' legal-term pun (Latin caput/head + feudal tenure + beheadings) is a recognised scholarly reading; the note correctly flags that 'droit du seigneur' was more satirical emblem than universal practice, which is appropriately cautious.

anchor_text: leave me at the White Hart in Southwark
summary: The White Hart was a real inn in Southwark, south of the Thames, and the documented headquarters of Cade's rebellion during the days the rebels held London in July 1450. Southwark, outside the city walls and the jurisdiction of the London aldermen, was a traditional gathering ground for armies, rebels, and those who wanted to avoid city authority.
detail: Holinshed names the White Hart as the inn where Cade lodged during the occupation of London. Its location in Southwark was significant: the district lay across London Bridge on the Surrey bank, technically outside the City of London's authority, and was home to theatres, bear-baiting arenas, and other enterprises the city fathers could not suppress. The rebel force camped there while raiding the city proper by day. Cade's reproach to his deserting followers — that they are leaving him at his own headquarters — is also a complaint that their defection is happening right in front of him.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Jack Cade lodging at the White Hart inn in Southwark, July 1450.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2582

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) names the White Hart inn in Southwark as Cade's lodging during the July 1450 occupation of London, and Southwark's extra-city status is historically accurate; the citation is genuine and supportive.

The identification of the White Hart as Cade's documented Southwark HQ, the explanation of Southwark's extra-city status, and the reading of Cade's complaint as a lament about being deserted at his own base are all defensible.

anchor_text: you are all recreants and dastards, and delight to live in slavery
summary: 'Recreant' means a coward who has surrendered or abandoned his cause — from the French se recreire, to yield in combat. A 'dastard' is a sneak-coward, someone who acts treacherously rather than facing danger openly. Cade hurls both words at the rebels who are defecting to the king's side, insisting that choosing royal pardon over the rebellion is not just betrayal but cowardice.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'recreant' and 'dastard.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2585

Onions' Shakespeare Glossary is a real and authoritative reference that covers both 'recreant' (defined as 'traitor', from Old French recroire meaning to yield in combat) and 'dastard' (coward, dastardly); the source exists and supports the lexical claim.

'Recreant' (yielded combatant, from Old French se recreire) and 'dastard' (coward acting by stealth) are correctly glossed, and the application to Cade's denunciation of the defecting rebels fits the text precisely.

anchor_text: whilst you live at jar The fearful French, whom you late vanquished, Should make a start o'er seas
summary: 'At jar' means in a state of quarrel or discord — the same root as the sound of a harsh, grating noise. Clifford argues that while the English are fighting one another, the very French they recently defeated will seize the chance to invade England. 'Make a start o'er seas' means to make a sudden advance across the Channel.
detail: The argument is rhetorically sharp: Clifford does not appeal to loyalty or law but to national shame and self-interest. The French have just been driven back (the play's backdrop is the final collapse of the English position in France after Cade's rebellion), so invoking their return as invaders is a live threat, not a distant one. 'Jar' in the sense of 'discord, disagreement' is common in the period; compare Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'jar.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'jar' (discord, quarrel).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2598
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (available via Perseus Digital Library) does contain an entry for 'jar' listing 'discord, quarrel, contention' as meanings, directly supporting the annotation's gloss.

'At jar' as discord is correct and well-attested; Clifford's argument that English civil strife invites a French counter-invasion is accurately read from the text, and the minor chronological imprecision in the detail note does not affect the gloss itself.

anchor_text: Crying 'Villiaco!' unto all they meet
summary: 'Villiaco' (also spelled 'Viliaco') is an Italian or Italianate term meaning 'coward' or 'base fellow' — roughly equivalent to calling someone a lowlife villain. Clifford paints a humiliating picture of the French swaggering through London streets and taunting Englishmen to their faces with this scornful word, daring them to do anything about it.
detail: The word is a borrowing from Italian vigliacco (coward, wretch). Clifford's image is deliberately provocative: the most shameful thing he can imagine is foreign invaders using a foreign insult to mock the English in their own capital. The appeal to national pride and shame does exactly what it is designed to do — the crowd switches allegiance back to the king within the same exchange.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'villiaco' (variant 'viliaco'): Italian vigliacco, a coward or base person; used as a term of contempt.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2603

The OED does carry an entry for 'villiaco' (variant 'viliaco') as an Italianate borrowing from vigliacco meaning a coward or base person, and the etymology and definition given in the annotation are accurate.

The derivation from Italian vigliacco (coward, wretch) and the reading of Clifford's image as a nationalistic shaming device — imagined French invaders taunting Englishmen in their own streets — are sound and consistent with the rhetorical logic of the speech.

anchor_text: Was ever feather so lightly blown to and fro as this multitude
summary: Cade compares the crowd to a feather blown back and forth by the wind — a simile for the commons' complete lack of political conviction. They chanted 'We'll follow Cade!' only moments before; now they shout 'A Clifford! we'll follow the king!' The image of the feather captures their weightlessness: they can be moved by whoever last spoke, not by any settled loyalty.
detail: The simile of the feather as emblem of inconstancy was proverbial in the period; to be 'light as a feather' was to be without substance or resolve. Cade's complaint is bitterly self-aware: he has built his entire movement on popular support, and now sees that support is worth nothing. The line is also quietly comic — the most dangerous rebel of the play is deflated by the sheer silliness of the mob he led. The 'many-headed multitude' as fickle, easily swayed, and ungovernable is a recurring anxiety in Shakespeare's history plays.

sources.name: Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England
sources.citation: Tilley, M. P. A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1950), F154 ('as light as a feather').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2612

Tilley's Dictionary of Proverbs (1950) is a real work and the feather/inconstancy proverb is genuine period material, but the specific entry number F154 cannot be verified through accessible sources and an independent search suggests the 'light as a feather' proverb may appear at a different F-number (possibly F150), making the precise citation unconfirmable.

The feather-as-inconstancy simile is proverbial, the annotation's reading of the crowd's oscillation (TLN 2578, 2590, 2610) is accurate, and characterizing Cade as bitterly self-aware about the worthlessness of popular support is a mainstream-defensible interpretation.

anchor_text: crept out of my cradle But I was made a king at nine months old
summary: Henry VI was crowned King of England at Windsor on 6 November 1429, when he was eight years old, not nine months. Shakespeare compresses the timeline for rhetorical effect: Henry was born 6 December 1421 and his father Henry V died 31 August 1422, making the infant king nine months old when he inherited the throne, not at his coronation. The line captures the central pathos of Henry's reign — he never knew anything but the burden of the crown.
detail: The historical infant king had two regencies: John, Duke of Bedford, governed France, and his uncle Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (the 'good Duke' now dead), served as Lord Protector in England during Henry's minority. Henry was formally crowned at Westminster Abbey in November 1429 (aged nearly eight), and in Paris in December 1431. Shakespeare collapses 'inherited at nine months' and 'crowned as a child' into a single image; the anachronism is deliberate and serves the portrait of a man who has never had the luxury of not being king. Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), records both the date of Henry V's death and the minority governance.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the death of Henry V (31 August 1422) and the minority governance of Henry VI.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2628

Holinshed 1587 is a real and appropriate source for Henry V's death (31 August 1422) and Henry VI's minority governance; the key dates (birth 6 December 1421, Westminster coronation 6 November 1429, Paris coronation December 1431) are all correct.

The claim that Henry inherited the throne at nine months is historically accurate (Henry V died August 1422, Henry VI born December 1421); the gloss correctly distinguishes inheritance from coronation and the label 'anachronism' is a minor misnomer but does not corrupt the interpretation.

anchor_text: humbly thus, with halters on their necks, Expect your highness' doom
summary: A 'halter' is a noose or rope used for hanging; wearing one around the neck was the traditional gesture by which rebels submitted to a lord and acknowledged they deserved execution. 'Doom' here means judgment or sentence — not necessarily death, though the word carries that threat. The rebels enter literally presenting themselves as condemned men, placing their lives in Henry's hands.
detail: The halter-submission was a recognized ritual of surrender with deep roots in English custom: the most famous instance, much discussed in Tudor history books, was the six burghers of Calais in 1347, who came barefoot with halters around their necks to surrender the city to Edward III (Froissart, Chronicles, Book I). The gesture communicates total submission and forefeiture of any claim to mercy as of right — the king may do as he pleases. Henry's pardon of the rebels (TLN 2640-2646) demonstrates his characteristic mercy, which the play consistently frames as both his best quality and part of his political weakness. 'Doom' in the sense of authoritative judgment persists in 'doomsday' and the legal term 'doom' (OED s.v. 'doom' n. 3).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'halter' n. 1a (a rope for leading or hanging); s.v. 'doom' n. 3 (sentence, judgment pronounced by authority).

sources.name: Froissart, Chronicles
sources.citation: Jean Froissart, Chronicles (trans. Berners, 1523-25), Book I, ch. 145: the halter-submission of the burghers of Calais, 1347 — the standard English example of the ritual.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2636

OED entries for 'halter' and 'doom' are real and supportive; Froissart Chronicles (trans. Berners, 1523-25), Book I, ch. 145 for the Calais burghers halter-submission is confirmed by the Wikipedia article on The Burghers of Calais, which cites exactly that chapter.

The halter-submission as a ritual of unconditional surrender is well attested; 'doom' as authoritative judgment is the plain Elizabethan sense; the Calais-burghers parallel is a recognised Tudor exemplum and does not overreach the textual evidence.

anchor_text: puissant and a mighty power Of gallowglasses and stout kerns
summary: 'Gallowglasses' (also 'galloglass') were heavily armored Irish or Scottish-Irish mercenary soldiers, typically armed with a long axe, who served Gaelic lords and could also be hired by English commanders. 'Kerns' were lightly armed Irish foot soldiers. Both terms were well known to Shakespeare's audience because English colonial ventures in Ireland, including the Nine Years' War (1593-1603), made Irish military forces a constant subject of news and anxiety. York, returning from his governorship of Ireland, brings these soldiers as his private army.
detail: The word 'gallowglass' comes from Irish Gaelic galloglach, literally 'foreign warrior'; gallowglasses were a distinct military class who emigrated from the Western Isles of Scotland to Ireland from the 13th century onward and were prized as shock troops. 'Kern' (Irish ceithearn, 'troop') denoted lighter skirmishers. Both types appear repeatedly in Elizabethan writing about Ireland: Edmund Spenser, A View of the Present State of Ireland (c. 1596, published 1633), describes them in detail. Shakespeare uses the same pairing in Macbeth (1.2: 'the merciless Macdonwald... from the western isles / Of kerns and gallowglasses is supplied'). York's ability to land an Irish army in England underscores that his months as the King's lieutenant in Ireland have given him independent military power — and a force outside the control of the English crown.

sources.name: Spenser, View of Ireland
sources.citation: Edmund Spenser, A View of the Present State of Ireland (c. 1596, published Dublin 1633), describing gallowglasses and kerns as distinct Irish military classes.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gallowglass' n. (Irish Gaelic galloglach, 'foreign warrior'); s.v. 'kern' n.1 (Irish ceithearn, lightly armed Irish foot soldier).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2650

Spenser's View of the Present State of Ireland (c. 1596, published Dublin 1633) is real and does describe gallowglasses and kerns as distinct Irish military classes; OED etymologies for both terms (galloglach / ceithearn) are accurate.

The etymology, military typology, and Macbeth parallel are all mainstream-defensible; the inference that York's Irish command gave him an army outside royal control is directly supported by the scene's dramatic logic.

anchor_text: Like to a ship that, having scap'd a tempest, Is straightway calm'd and boarded with a pirate
summary: Henry uses an extended simile (a comparison introduced by 'like to') to describe his political position: Cade's rebellion was the storm that threatened to sink him, but no sooner has it passed than York arrives with an army — the 'pirate' who boards a ship becalmed and helpless after the storm. 'Calm'd' means brought to a dead calm (no wind to sail away), leaving the vessel motionless and vulnerable. The image captures Henry's sense that he cannot catch a moment of safety.
detail: The simile is a compressed version of the 'ship of state' topos that runs throughout the history plays (compare 2 Henry VI 3.1: 'The commons, like an angry hive of bees... / Shall all in general call thee king, / And bid thee from the sea-shore go'). What makes it precise here is 'calm'd': after a tempest, a ship that survives the violence may be left with no wind at all, stranded and unable to maneuver — the worst moment for a pirate to appear. Henry's situation after Cade is exactly this: he has just survived a crisis that exhausted his political energy, and York strikes while he has no momentum. The figure also carries ironic resonance: York himself is a 'pirate' in the play's terms, just as the actual pirates who seized and beheaded Suffolk earlier in Act 4 were literal versions of predators who board weakened ships.

sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'calm' vb. (to make a dead calm, to becalm a vessel).

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
