fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2657

Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75) is a real work with the correct dates and does cover 'calm' as a verb meaning to becalm; Holinshed 1587 is a real and appropriate source for York's return from Ireland with armed forces.

The core simile — storm survived, ship becalmed and boarded — is read correctly; the 'ironic resonance' linking York to Suffolk's killers in the detail note overreaches (the play draws no such connection), but the summary-level interpretation is sound and that elaboration does not corrupt the annotation's claim.

anchor_text: brain-pain had been cleft with a brown bill
summary: A 'brown bill' was a long-handled infantry weapon — a type of halberd or bill-hook — whose metal head was left unpolished (hence 'brown,' meaning oxidized rather than bright-blued steel). It was the standard weapon of English foot-soldiers and constables through the sixteenth century. Cade is saying that without a helmet, his skull would have been split open in battle.
detail: Bills were cutting weapons descended from agricultural tools, mounted on poles six to eight feet long; 'brown' distinguished unpolished iron from the more expensive 'black' (painted) or 'bright' (polished) metal. By Shakespeare's time the brown bill was associated with the watch and lower infantry, and its frequent mention in the plays marks a speaker as a common soldier or watchman rather than a gentleman with a sword. The weapon appears again at 4 Henry VI 2.3 and elsewhere in the histories.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'brown bill' (a bill-weapon of unpolished iron; used by English foot-soldiers and watchmen, 15th-17th c.).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'bill' and 'brown bill.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2685
OED and Onions both attest 'brown bill' as an unpolished pole-arm (bill-weapon) used by English foot-soldiers and the watch in the 15th–17th centuries, fully supporting the annotation's claims.

The gloss is accurate: 'brown bill' denotes a long-handled bill-weapon of unpolished iron associated with foot-soldiers and watchmen, and the OED and Onions both support this; the contrast with the helmet (sallet) is textually clear.

anchor_text: I seek not to wax great by others' waning
summary: Iden's opening speech is a deliberate counter-image to everything happening in the play: while the court tears itself apart and Jack Cade's rebellion burns London, this Kentish squire is content with a small inheritance, asks for no more than he has, and sends the poor away satisfied. The line 'I seek not to wax great by others' waning' directly repudiates the way every lord in the play advances himself by ruining rivals. Shakespeare sets the contented garden against the chaos of a kingdom without order.
detail: The speech echoes the Stoic-Christian ideal of the 'retired life' that runs through the history plays: the Bishop of Carlisle's reproach to the ambitious in Richard II, Henry VI's 'O God! methinks it were a happy life / To be no better than a homely swain' in 3 Henry VI (2.5), and the garden scene of Richard II (3.4) where the gardeners stand for wise husbandry of the realm. Iden's garden is the play's last image of order before the battle of St Albans opens the Wars of the Roses. That a private gentleman's virtue survives when the state has collapsed is both comforting and damning as a comment on the court. The great-chain-of-being doctrine held that every degree should perform its proper function; Iden is the one figure who does.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the aftermath of Cade's rebellion and the subsequent unrest in Kent.

sources.name: Tillyard, The Elizabethan World Picture
sources.citation: E. M. W. Tillyard, The Elizabethan World Picture (1943), on degree, order, and the pastoral ideal in the histories.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2693

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) covers the aftermath of Cade's rebellion in Kent, and Tillyard's Elizabethan World Picture (Chatto & Windus, 1943) is a genuine, well-known scholarly work treating degree, order, and the pastoral ideal in the histories.

The pastoral-versus-court contrast and the chain-of-being framing are defensible mainstream readings, but the annotation over-reaches in claiming this is the play's 'last image of order before the battle of St Albans opens the Wars of the Roses' — that framing imposes Tillyard's 1943 providential-history thesis, which has been substantially contested since the 1980s (Rackin, Hodgdon, Grady), and presenting it as uncontroversial 'high' confidence overstates scholarly consensus

anchor_text: entering his fee-simple without leave
summary: 'Fee-simple' is a legal term for absolute freehold ownership of land — ownership with no conditions or time limit, freely inherited by heirs. Cade uses it sarcastically to mock Iden as 'the lord of the soil': he knows he is trespassing on the man's outright private property. The phrase shows Cade's comic awareness of the legal system he spent the rebellion trying to destroy.
detail: In English property law 'fee simple' (from Old French fief simple) is the highest form of land ownership, carrying the right to sell, bequeath, or mortgage freely. The irony is characteristic: Cade spent Act 4 ordering the burning of records and the death of lawyers, yet here he precisely names the property right he has violated. The aside is also a reminder that Iden is a private gentleman, not a government agent — Cade has wandered not onto crown land or a lord's estate but into a private freeholder's garden.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'fee simple' (absolute freehold; the most complete form of heritable land ownership in English law).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'fee-simple.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2698
OED and Onions correctly document 'fee simple' as absolute heritable freehold ownership, the highest form of land tenure in English law.

The legal definition of fee-simple as absolute freehold is correct and well-attested, and the irony that Cade — destroyer of lawyers and records — uses a precise legal term for his trespass is a legitimate and mainstream critical observation.

anchor_text: best blood that ever was broached
summary: 'Broached' here means tapped or drawn, as wine is drawn from a cask by piercing it with a spigot. To 'broach' blood is to shed it by piercing the body — the same image as tapping a barrel. Cade swears his defiance 'by the best blood that ever was broached': the highest blood ever spilled, with a tavern-keeper's relish for the image.
detail: The verb 'broach' (from Old French brochier, to pierce with a spit or tap) was used in butchery and wine-keeping for piercing a cask or a carcass; in violent contexts it means to wound so that blood flows freely. The phrasing is deliberately low and physical — Cade consistently fuses the kitchen with the battlefield, and this oath carries the same double flavor as his sallet puns. The exact referent of 'best blood' is deliberately vague: it could be Christ's blood (a blasphemous oath by the Passion), noble blood, or simply the finest blood spilled in any fight — Cade's rhetoric habitually inflates itself without fixing its meaning.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'broach' v. sense 3: to pierce (a cask) so as to draw liquor; hence, to shed (blood).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'broach' (to tap a cask; to shed blood).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2709
OED 'broach' v. records the sense of piercing a cask to draw liquor and, figuratively, shedding blood; Onions likewise attests both senses, fully supporting the annotation's etymology and gloss.

The cask-tapping sense of 'broach' is well-established, the etymological derivation is sound, and noting the deliberate ambiguity of the referent (Christ's blood, noble blood, or any great blood shed) is a fair and defensible reading rather than an over-reach.

anchor_text: the unconquered soul of Cade is fled
summary: Cade's dying speech is a study in comic-heroic self-delusion: he declares he was not beaten in battle but 'slain' by famine, curses the garden that will become a burial ground, and exits proclaiming his soul 'unconquered.' In the de casibus tradition — the 'fall of princes' genre — a great man toppled from prosperity to ruin was a tragedy; Cade applies the same tragic language to himself though his 'greatness' was a pretense from the start. The gap between the grandiose claim and the starving reality is the scene's central irony.
detail: Cade is one of Shakespeare's most sustained examples of a man who narrates himself as the hero of a story he is losing. His rebellion was the Duke of York's tool (3.1); his army deserted him for a royal pardon; he dies not by sword but by five days without food. Yet his last words reach for the cadences of a Roman general. The 'wither, garden' curse echoes stage convention for dying tyrants — but Cade is no tyrant, just a hungry man with a sword. Shakespeare uses the language of de casibus tragedy (the great soul departing) to deflate rather than honour, showing how the rebel's rhetoric was always more borrowed than genuine.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Cade's death in a garden in Kent after his army deserted him.

sources.name: Boccaccio; A Mirror for Magistrates
sources.citation: Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360); A Mirror for Magistrates (1559) — the de casibus tradition of the fallen great man.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2737

Holinshed (1587) records Cade's death in Kent after his army's desertion; Boccaccio's De Casibus (core composed c. 1355–60, revised to 1374 — 'c. 1360' is an acceptable approximation) and A Mirror for Magistrates (first edition 1559) are both genuine works establishing the de casibus tradition cited.

The ironic application of de casibus heroic-exit language to a starving rebel is a sound and mainstream critical observation; Cade's dying claim of an 'unconquered soul' is undercut by the stage fact that he was beaten in single combat after days of starvation, and the gap between rhetoric and reality is clearly the scene's point.

anchor_text: wear it as a herald's coat, To emblaze the honour
summary: A herald's coat (a 'coat of arms' or tabard) was the heraldic garment blazoned with a noble family's armorial bearings, worn by the herald who proclaimed tournaments and delivered formal messages. 'Emblaze' means to display or proclaim heraldically — to blazon, to make brilliantly public. Iden plans to hang his blood-stained sword over his tomb as a permanent, honorable display of his deed, the way a coat of arms advertised a family's history and worth.
detail: Heralds were officials of the College of Arms who recorded genealogies, designed and granted coats of arms, and wore embroidered tabards bearing the royal arms at public ceremonies. Their 'coat' was thus both a garment and a walking advertisement of heraldic identity. 'Emblaze' conflates 'blaze' (to proclaim aloud, as heralds did) and 'blazon' (to describe or depict armorial bearings). Iden imagines the Cade-blood as if it were heraldic tincture — a permanent mark of earned, publicly recorded honor. The speech elevates a garden killing into a chivalric trophy, anticipating the knighthood Iden receives in 5.1. 'Emblaze' (also spelled 'emblazon') is first recorded in this sense in the late sixteenth century; Onions cites the passage.

anchor_text: like to Achilles' spear, Is able with the change to kill and cure

anchor_text: It is great sin to swear unto a sin, But greater sin to keep a sinful oath
summary: Salisbury advances a moral-theological argument: an oath sworn in support of a wrong cause is itself sinful, and performing it compounds the sin rather than excusing it. He is arguing that his oath of allegiance to Henry is void because Henry is not the rightful king. The logic was genuinely debated by medieval and Renaissance theologians; it would strike first audiences as dangerously convenient for a traitor but not obviously wrong as a matter of church doctrine.

Thomas Aquinas and later Protestant divines agreed that an oath to commit a crime binds no one (Summa Theologica II-II Q.89 a.7). But applying it to an allegiance oath to a reigning, anointed king was politically explosive: it is precisely the argument Henry VIII's opponents used against the oath of supremacy, and it licenses anyone who judges a king illegitimate to defect. The playwright seems to let Salisbury have the better of the argument while making Queen Margaret's counter-speech ('A subtle traitor needs no sophister') the audience's gut-check.

anchor_text: A dreadful lay!--Address thee instantly

Young Clifford's grief tips into a death-wish for creation itself — a grief so private it demands the end of the world.

'Chair-days' is Young Clifford's own coinage, unique to this play: it evokes the fireside chair of a peaceful old age, as opposed to a battlefield. The contrast — that a man who survived to white hair should have the right to quiet ease — sharpens the outrage at his father's death.

anchor_text: as wild Medea young Absyrtus did
summary: Medea was a sorceress of Greek myth who killed her own younger brother Absyrtus, cut his body into pieces, and scattered the fragments to delay her father's pursuit. Young Clifford swears he will cut York infants into 'gobbets' (chunks of flesh) just as ruthlessly — using one of antiquity's most extreme images of calculated cruelty.

The episode was notorious in Renaissance reading as the type of cold, calculating savagery — Medea commits fratricide not in passion but as a tactical maneuver. Young Clifford's application of it is chilling: he will kill babies of the house of York not in rage but as deliberate, systematic revenge, 'In cruelty will I seek out my fame' (TLN 3035). This vow foreshadows his murder of York's young son Rutland in 3 Henry VI 1.3.

anchor_text: As did Aeneas old Anchises bear, So bear I thee upon my manly shoulders
summary: Young Clifford lifts his dead father's body from the battlefield as Aeneas carried his aged father Anchises out of burning Troy on his shoulders — the classical image of devoted filial duty. But he points out the crucial difference: 'Aeneas bare a living load'; his father is dead weight.

Shakespeare's audience knew it from school Latin and from Marlowe and Nashe's Dido, Queen of Carthage (c. 1587-88), which dramatizes it directly. Young Clifford invokes it to elevate what he is doing to the highest register of filial love, then deflates the allusion with the pointed contrast: the great Trojan act was a rescue of a living man; this is a removal of a corpse. The word 'nothing' — 'Nothing so heavy as these woes of mine' — is the scene's most compressed grief.

summary: Richard Plantagenet notes that Somerset has been killed beneath the sign of an alehouse called the Castle — fulfilling the prophecy made earlier in the play that Somerset should 'shun castles.' The spirit conjured by the witch Margery Jourdain told him to avoid castles; Somerset, dying under a painted inn-sign, cannot escape even a picture of one. Shakespeare uses the coincidence — not found in Holinshed — to pay off the prophecy ironically: the warning was real but unheeded, and even a painted castle kills him. anchor_text: Can we outrun the heavens? good Margaret, stay
summary: Henry's passive question — can we outrun heaven's will? — against Margaret's furious practicality ('Away, my lord! you are slow') captures the play's central contrast: the king who defers to God's providence and does nothing, and the queen who acts. The exchange shows who really commands the Lancastrian side as the battle is lost.

Margaret's blunt 'What are you made of? you'll nor fight nor fly' is the clearest statement in the play of how she, not he, has become the effective head of the Lancastrian party. The scene is brief but essential: it establishes the dynamic that will dominate 3 Henry VI, where Margaret leads armies while Henry sits on a hill watching the battle and philosophizes. Henry's passivity is rooted historically in his known piety and suspected mental incapacity; Shakespeare dramatizes it as a governing contrast with his warrior-queen.

anchor_text: winter lion, who in rage forgets
summary: York calls the elderly Salisbury a 'winter lion' — a man in the winter of his life who, in the heat of battle, forgets the bruises and wearing of old age ('aged contusions and all brush of time') and fights with a young man's fury. The image fuses the lion's traditional ferocity with the paradox of an old fighter animated by rage.

Describing Salisbury as a 'winter lion' does not weaken him; winter is the season that tests endurance, and the phrase implies that his courage, like a lion in winter, is all the more remarkable for the hardship it overcomes. 'Contusions' (bruises, injuries) and 'brush of time' (the wear and abrasion of years) are the bodily costs he ignores. York's opening speech establishes Salisbury as the indispensable moral weight of the Yorkist cause — if Salisbury is lost, the day itself is not theirs.

anchor_text: call a present court of parliament. / Let us pursue him ere the writs go forth
summary: A 'writ' was the royal legal summons that formally convened a parliament; once issued, members were bound to appear and the session had legal force. York's urgency is political: if Henry reaches London and gets the writs out before the Yorkists arrive, he can use parliament to put the realm legally back under Lancaster's control. The race to London is as much a race to control the law as it is a military pursuit.

A sitting parliament was a formidable instrument of royal legitimacy: it could attaint traitors, vote taxes for an army, and issue proclamations. York's calculation is precise — he must reach London before Henry can use this machinery against him. Holinshed records that after the battle of St Albans the Yorkists did indeed accompany the king to London, where they secured custody of his person and effectively controlled the next parliament (November 1455). The phrase 'present court' means an immediately convened session, not a regular one.

anchor_text: our forefathers had no other books but the score and the tally
summary: Before paper records were widespread, debts and transactions were kept on tally sticks: a notched wooden rod split lengthwise so creditor and debtor each kept a matching half (the 'tally'). A 'score' (from the Old Norse for 'notch') is one of those cut marks, and 'score' in the sense of twenty derives from counting up to that number of notches. Cade's point is that honest, illiterate Englishmen kept their accounts faithfully without paper — printing and grammar schools are corruptions, not improvements.

When the old sticks were finally burned in 1834, the fire spread and destroyed much of the Palace of Westminster (the Houses of Parliament). The episode underlines how genuinely ancient the practice Cade romanticizes was — and how recently it survived even in later England.

anchor_text: mightst as well have known all our names as thus to name the several colours we do wear
summary: Gloucester's proof is genuine: a person born blind who had just received sight for the first time would have no way to link color-words to visual impressions they had never had. Gloucester's cross-examination is a two-stage proof: sight distinguishes colors, but knowing whose name belongs to which person requires prior knowledge, which Simpcox denies having.

anchor_text: this Edmund, in the reign of Bolingbroke, As I have read, laid claim unto the crown; And, but for Owen Glendower, had been king
summary: Salisbury recalls Edmund Mortimer, whose line had a rival claim to Henry IV (Bolingbroke). Owen Glendower was a Welsh lord who launched a major uprising against Henry IV from 1400 and allied with the English rebels (including Hotspur Percy). Shakespeare dramatized Glendower and Mortimer fully in Henry IV Part 1. 'As I have read' signals that Salisbury is reconstructing a written, genealogical case, not living memory.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March, his claim under Henry IV, and Owen Glendower's Welsh rebellion (c. 1400-1415) — the source whose conflation of the two Edmund Mortimers Shakespeare follows.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 921

Holinshed (1587) conflates the uncle Sir Edmund Mortimer (the rebel captured by Glendower) with his nephew Edmund the 5th Earl of March (the claimant), precisely as Shakespeare does; the annotation accurately reflects the Holinshed narrative Shakespeare was following.

Rescued in 2026-06-01 review sweep — Interp judge flagged that the gloss conflated the two Edmund Mortimers; reworded to make clear the play and its source (Holinshed) deliberately merge them, which is itself the point — and the source judge confirmed Holinshed does exactly this.

detail: Following his chronicle source, Salisbury runs together two real men both named Edmund Mortimer — Edmund, Earl of March (the dynastic claimant) and Sir Edmund Mortimer (the one actually captured by Glendower) — and treats them as a single figure. Holinshed makes the same conflation, so the 'error' faithfully reproduces Shakespeare's source rather than misstating it.
